Let us not proudly glory against the broken branches; let us rather reflect by whose grace it is, and by much mercy, and on what root, we have been grafted into.

Here he places the calling of the Jews after the conversion of the gentiles has occurred: speaking either in the person of the prophet or in the person of the gentiles, that they may be in the tail who were in the head: "blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in" (Rom 11:25). "Let us walk," at the same time and in agreement, that there may be one sheepfold: "and there shall be one fold and one shepherd" (John 10:16). "In the light": "Walk whilst you have the light" (John 12:35).

Such are his prophecies about all the Gentiles. Hear what he proceeds to add about the Jews:

" 6. For he has rejected his people, the house of the God of Jacob, for the land is filled as at the beginning with auguries, as the land of strangers, and many children of strangers are born to them. 7. For the land was filled with silver and gold, and there was no end of their treasures."

And that which follows after this, to which he adds:

"9. And they worshipped that which their own fingers had made, and a man bowed down, and was humbled, and I will not reject them. 10. And now enter ye into the rocks, and hide yourselves in the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord, and from the face of his glory, when he arises to shake the earth."

And in this he teaches that there will be a Resurrection of the Lord, at which all the land of the Jewish people will be shattered. For the whole portion refers to them, in the following sections as well, saying : "For the day of the Lord of Sabaoth shall be upon every one that is proud and insolent, and upon every one that is lofty and exalted." And that which follows. Wherefore it is on the day of the Lord's Resurrection, that the prophet having first addressed those who lift themselves up against the knowledge of God, says: "On this very day"; "the Lord shall be exalted in that very day, and they shall hide all the work of their hands, bearing them into the caves," clearly showing the destruction of the idols, which the Jews themselves and all other men cast away after the appearance of the Saviour, despising all superstitions :

" 20. On that day, he says, a man shall cast away his abominations of gold and silver which they made to worship vanities."

Thus speaking, it would seem, generally about all men, because of the coming call of the Gentiles.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

Because they have been filled of old, and have had soothsayers, like the Philistines. For Philistines the Seventy always translated foreigners, a common noun for a proper one: this is today the nation of the Palestinians, as it were of the Philisthinians, because the Hebrew tongue does not have the letter P, but uses the Greek PHI in its place. Hence what is said in the Psalms, with the enumeration of the other nations, The foreigners have been made subject to me (Ps 59 [60]:10), signifies not all foreign nations but properly the Palestinians. And he gives the reasons why God has cast off his people, the house of Jacob: because they have been filled, he says, as they were at the beginning, with soothsayers and omens and all the filth of idolatry. We know from the writing of Moses that the omens and auguries which the nations had whom the Lord drove out before Israel, the Canaanites, Amorites and Hittites, were not to be heeded. The commentators of the Church expound this passage in one way and another. For some will have it to signify that, the people of the Jews having been cast off, the Roman army entered the land once of promise, and, the Jews being expelled, foreigners dwelt in Judea, settlers of diverse nations from the whole world, brought in by Titus and Vespasian and Hadrian and the other emperors. Others, however, think that this does not pertain to Roman times but to earlier ones, before they were laid waste by the Babylonians, because they are related to have lived under impious kings and were forsaken by the Lord.

And they have clung to strange boys. For which the Seventy translated: And many foreign sons were born to them. Symmachus: And with strange sons they applauded. For which there is written in the Hebrew JESPHICU (ישפיקו), which the Hebrews interpret ἐσφηνώθησαν, and we have rendered they have clung, so that the shamefulness of the vices in the Jewish nation may be shown. And the Greeks and the Romans once suffered from this vice to such a degree that even the most famous philosophers of Greece kept male concubines publicly; and Hadrian, learned in the arts of philosophy, consecrated Antinous as a god and established a temple, victims and priests for him, and from him a city and a region of Egypt received its name. Among the harlots too, in the arches of the theaters, boys stood exposed to public lust, until under the emperor Constantine, when the Gospel of Christ shone forth, both the unbelief of all the nations and this shamefulness were done away. The Seventy, however, signify that their wives were violated, in bearing strange sons to the Jews. Symmachus, by a certain circumlocution and in the decent word of applauding, has shown the same shamefulness with boys.

Here he shows their guilt. And first, in general, second, in particular, at: "and have had soothsayers."

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he shows their separation from God, when he says, "for you have cast off," and, as the Gloss continues, rightly are they to be called, because you have cast off. "Why are they cast out, he and his seed, and are cast into a land which they know not?" (Jer 22:28). Second, he places the reason for their separation, because, namely, "they are filled," with iniquity, "as in times past," in Egypt. "The land is full of adulterers" (Jer 23:10). For there is no cause of separation from God except sin; hence below: "your sins have divided between you and your God" (Isa 59:2).

Here he sets out their fault in particular, and especially concerning idolatry, which he denounces in them in three ways. First, as to the gentile way of life; second, as to the occasion of idolatry, where it says, "their land is filled with silver and gold" (Isa 2:7); third, as to the observation of worship, where it says, "and their land is filled" (Isa 2:8).

He censures them for the gentile way of life in two matters. First, as to the diviners and soothsayers that they had: hence he says: "soothsayers," that is, those who foretell the future from the cry and chirping of birds, as the Philistines, among whom this superstition flourished most, against what is commanded in Deuteronomy 18:9: "beware lest you have a mind to imitate the abominations of those nations," and immediately below this, "let there be not found among you any one that consults soothsayers, or observes dreams and omens" (Deut 18:10).

But it seems that augury is not a sin. For birds have a better estimation than fish who are more aquatic; but mariners obtain predictions of a coming storm from the movement of certain fish: therefore something also may be foretold concerning the future through birds. And to this is to be said that God foresaw what was necessary for each thing to be preserved in being, according to the capacity of its nature; and therefore to man he gave reason, through which, by comparing, he is able to devise for himself remedies against harmful things. And because reason is lacking in brute animals, he ordained that nature should supply what is lacking from reason; and therefore weapons and coverings, which man must acquire for himself through art, are given to animals by nature. Similarly, a certain power of natural estimation was also created for them, impelling them to carry out the activity of their species; hence it is better to say that they are acted upon than that they act, as John Damascene says; and when an inferior nature is regulated by a superior nature and is moved, impressions are left in them of superior movements rubbing such movement by which they are moved to provide for themselves in necessities. And obtaining a prediction in such things from birds or the movements of birds or of other animals is not a sin, but only about those things which have their cause from free will, which does not operate by the necessity of the stars.

Second, he censures them as to unnatural passions, in which they were subject: hence he says: "to strange children," that is, foreign, or strange to God, "have adhered," through filthy abuse. "Men with men, working that which is filthy" (Rom 1:27). In 2 Maccabees 4:13, it is said of this vice, "now this was an increase, and progress of heathenish and foreign manners, through the abominable and unheard of wickedness of Jason, that impious wretch, and no priest."

Someone might ask, what is wrong with having silver or horses, particularly when what the people believed was not rigorous? How should we respond? The prophet was not criticizing the use of these possessions but the misuse of them. When he said, "Woe to the mighty," he was not condemning them for having possessions but for hoarding so much more than they needed.

And the land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end of its treasures. Among the other vices of the land of the house of Jacob is numbered also the abundance of gold and silver. Among omens and soothsayers, horses and chariots, which God forbade the kings of Israel to multiply, among idols, which are the works of men's hands, avarice is condemned. Hence the Lord commanded in the Gospel that we should not lay up for ourselves treasures on earth, and that we should not make treasures from which a thief can snatch, adding at the last: You cannot serve God and mammon (Matt 6:24). And finely has the Prophet expressed in other words that phrase of the little verse, The greedy man is ever in want, saying: And there is no end of its treasures; not that treasures have no end, but that the mind of those who possess them is not filled. And by these words both nations, the Jews and the Romans, are branded for avarice. Which the histories too, Greek as well as Latin, relate: that nothing is more avaricious than the nation of the Jews and of the Romans. Hence too the law on extortion was established, and daily we see that word of the Apostle fulfilled: You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? (Rom 2:21). A more thievish judge hears and condemns a thief, pronouncing in another's case a sentence upon himself.

And its land is filled with horses, and its chariots are innumerable. For what is possessed against God's command is not worthy of number. Hence it is said in the Psalms: The horse is deceptive for safety (Ps 32 [33]:17). And in Exodus: The horse and the rider he has thrown into the sea (Exod 15:1). And in another psalm: Some in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God (Ps 19 [20]:8). Both can be understood: that the people of the Jews multiplied horses and chariots for themselves against God's precept, and that the land of Judea was filled with the horses and chariots of the conquerors.

Vanity is the general term for vices, but vain in the particular sense means that which is found alien to God. Just as trusting in the Godhead is fruitful constancy, so deviating from him is the vanity that perishes.… So those who burned with the most base love of idols are convicted, and the phrase is to be pronounced as a rebuke, as if the words were, "Why do you love the vanity by which you perish?" We ought to love things that are beneficial, not harmful, for it is better to curse the things that cause the punishment of lasting damnation to afflict us.

Here he sets out the occasion of idolatry, which is avarice or its likeness: "or covetousness, which is a serving of idols" (Eph 5:3–5).

First, therefore, he shows their avarice as to the multiplication of things which pertain to the necessities of life, when he says, "their land is filled," in which is indicated the abundance of things; "and there is no end," in which is indicated the insatiability of the covetous man, who is not satisfied with money. "A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money: and he that loves riches shall reap no fruit from them" (Eccl 5:9), and: "I gave them corn, and wine, and oil, and silver, and I multiplied for them, and gold, which they have used in the service of Baal" (Hos 2:8).

Second, he shows their avarice as to things which pertain to transportation, where he says, "filled with horses." "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will call upon the name of the Lord, our God" (Ps 20:7).

Not only do human beings "make gods for themselves" from statues, but you will also find them "making gods for themselves" from their imaginations. For such people can imagine another god and creator of the world in a system different from the divine plan of the world recorded by the Spirit, other than the true world. These all have "made gods for themselves," and they have "worshiped the works of their hands." So, too, I believe is the case either among the Greeks who generate opinions, so to speak, of this philosophy or that, or among the heretics, the first who generate opinions. These have "made idols for themselves" and figments of the soul, and by turning to them "they worship the works of their hands," since they accept as truth their own fabrications.

And its land is filled with idols; they have worshiped the work of their own hands, what their fingers have made; and man has bowed himself down, and the man has been humbled. Where once was the Temple and the worship of God, there the statue of Hadrian and the idol of Jupiter were set up. Which many interpret of that testimony which we read in the Gospel: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place (Mark 13:14). And they bowed down to the work of their hands, and man, a rational animal, worshiped bronze and stone. But there are those who interpret these things of the Jews, that before they were taken by the Babylonians they did all these things, and were therefore abandoned by God. Hence at the end of the chapter too is set: Do not, therefore, forgive them. We can say this too according to the anagogy, that every doctrine contrary to the truth worships the works of its own hands and sets up idols in its land, and man bows down and the man is humbled and cannot raise himself up, because he is bound by the devil, unless the Lord raises him up, after the example of that woman whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, so that she could by no means look at the sky but always at the earth (Luke 13).

Here he denounces in them the worship of idolatry; and he adds to the weight of this from three things.

First, from its multitude, where he says, "also is full": "Ephraim has made many altars to sin" (Hos 7:11); "under every green tree, and on every high hill you didst prostitute yourself" (Jer 2:20).

Second, from the worthlessness of the idols: for they are "the work of their own hands," and still more, "which their own fingers have made." "The idols of the Gentiles are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men" (Ps 115:4).

Do not, therefore, forgive them. For which the Seventy translated: And I will not forgive them. If God is speaking, it is to be understood thus: Because they have done such things, I will not spare them, nor will I forgive such innumerable sins. If the Prophet, it is to be taken thus: Do not, therefore, forgive those who have committed such crimes. And if we understand it of the Romans, the interpretation is truer: who, overthrowing the temple of God, did not worship him who gave them the victory, but the idols of their own hands. But if of the Jews, it is a fierce sentence of the Prophet, so that he seems to pray against his own people, to whom he had said above: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.

Third, from the dignity of man: and therefore he says: "man," who was made to the image of God, "has bowed himself down," in putting himself under idols; "man," who seems powerful as to acquired things, "has been debased": "man when he was in honor did not understand; he is compared to senseless beasts, and is become like to them" (Ps 49:12). Below: "he bows down before it, and adores it, and prays unto it, saying: deliver me" (Isa 44:17).

"Therefore forgive them not." Here he threatens them with punishment. And this is divided into two parts: in the first part, he shows them that danger is imminent; in the second part, he closes the remedy of escape, where it says, "cease therefore from the man" (Isa 2:22).

He shows them that danger is imminent, by taking away three things: first, presumption of divine mercy; second, confidence in their own power, where it says, "the lofty eyes of man are humbled" (Isa 2:11); third, the remedy which remained in confidence in other gods, where it says, "in that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver" (Isa 2:20).

And because divine mercy has no measure, but always exalts itself above judgment (Jas 2:13), he does not remove it by foretelling that it will fail but by calling it down as just. Therefore he does two things. First, he places the calling down, saying: since they do such filthy evils, "therefore forgive them not," as if to say: would that there were justice, that you might have mercy on them in nothing: "shall I not visit for these things, says the Lord? And shall not my soul take revenge on such a nation?" (Jer 5:9).

Enter into the rock, hide yourself in the dug-out ground from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty. I indeed exhorted the people, saying, House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. But because the Lord has cast off the people of Jacob, and has cast them off because they either did or suffered the things which we have expounded above, therefore I foretell to you the evils that are to come, and I exhort you to enter the rocks and hide in the caves from the face of the Babylonian or the Roman army, when all things will be laid waste, according to what we read in the Gospel: Then they will say to the mountains, Fall upon us; and to the rocks, Hide us (Luke 23:30). But according to the anagogy we are commanded, before the face of the Lord's majesty, to take on the strength of the rock, of which it is said: The rock is a refuge for the hares (Ps 103 [104]:18); and, On a rock you have exalted me (Ps 26 [27]:6). Moses too is set in a cleft of the rock to see the back parts of God (Exod 33). And, The people drank from the spiritual rock that followed them (1 Cor 10:4). And he hides himself in the rock who enters his chamber and, having shut the door, adores the Father, so that, though placed in an earthly body, he does not feel the passing storm of the world.

Second, he places, ironically, the counsel to escape, saying, "enter you"; as if to say, since he himself does not send you away, it remains that you should hide yourself from his face. "Enter you into the rock," literally, into the fissures of the rocks to remain there; "hide you in the pit," that is, in the caverns of the earth, "from the face of the fear of the Lord," that is, from the face of those through whom God proves that he is to be feared and glorified: "leave the cities" (Jer 48:28); but this does not avail them, hence in Psalm 139:7: "whither shall I go from your spirit? Or whither shall I flee from your face?"

Bernard explains this as referring to Christ. "And the rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4); one must enter him through the affection of devotion. Therefore, Bernard says: that which is lacking to me I usurp from the heart of Jesus Christ. For out of his heart mercies overflow, and there is no lack of fissures by which they flow out: for they dug holes in his hands, pierced his feet. "Arise, make haste, my love, and come in the clefts of the rock" (Song 2:13–14).

The lofty eyes of man are humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down; but the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. When the enemies have come, and the Babylonian or Roman sword has laid waste the whole province, and the columns of warriors have besieged Jerusalem, then neither riches nor nobility of birth nor the power of offices will be able to defend anyone; but there will be one captivity for all, and God alone will be exalted, whose wrath no one will be able to avoid. Many understand these things of the day of judgment: that every creature, in comparison with the divine glory, will be humbled and bowed down, and will feel itself to be nothing.

Here he takes away from them confidence in their own power, and concerning this, he does two things: first, he excludes the power of resistance; second, he rejects the precaution of hiding, where it says, "and they shall go into the holes of rocks" (Isa 2:19).

He sets out two things to exclude the power of resistance. First, their lowering, both as to pride of heart, when he says, "the eyes," that is, pride, "of the lofty," that is, of powerful men, "are humbled," that is, they will be humbled: the past tense is used for the future because of the certitude of the prophecy: "a generation, whose eyes are lofty, and their eyelids lifted up on high" (Prov 30:13); "he will look on all that are proud, and confound them, and crush the wicked in their place" (Job 40:7). Then also as to nobility of ancestry; hence he says, "the height of men," that is, their nobility of ancestry: "yet I cast out the Amorrhite before their face: whose height was like the height of cedars" (Amos 2:9).

Second, he places the exaltation of the one who punishes: "the Lord alone shall be exalted," that is he who seemed weak in expectation, will appear high in punishing: "the Lord shall be known when he executes judgments" (Ps 9:16); below: "the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment" (Isa 5:16).

For the day of the Lord of hosts is upon everyone proud and lofty, and upon everyone arrogant. These things too are joined to the former. In that day, he says, in which the Lord alone will be exalted, that is, in the day of the Lord's vengeance, all the lofty and the arrogant and the high will be subjected to captivity and the sword. Μεταφορικῶς the word is about the great and the princes: that the more they have been proud, the more they are brought low. For the Lord resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5). Those who understand it of the day of judgment think that the devil is called proud and lofty and high and arrogant; who in his pride says: I will set my seat above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the lofty mountain, above all the lofty mountains, toward the North; I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High (Isa 14:13, 14): when out of the mouth of infants and sucklings praise will be perfected, that the enemy and the avenger may be destroyed (Ps 8:3).

Here is set out the manner of fulfillment of the things that have been predicted. And first, as to the lowering of men; second, as to the subtraction of things, where it says, "and upon all" (Isa 2:13).

Thus he says first: therefore this will be which was said, because "the day of the Lord," that is, the time of vengeance, below: "the day of vengeance is in my heart, the year of my redemption is come" (Isa 63:4); "of hosts," that there be no doubt about victory of him, under whom there is such a multitude of servants; he will come as heavy weight to compress, "upon every one that is proud and high-minded," that is, upon him who is raised up more from the great things he has; "and upon every one that is arrogant," who is elevated because of that which he does not have. The arrogant man is he who attributes to himself what he does not have (Gregory). "I hate arrogance, and pride, and every wicked way, and a mouth with a double tongue" (Prov 8:13). "And he shall be humbled": "he that exalts himself shall be humbled" (Luke 14:11).

And upon all the cedars of Lebanon, high and lifted up, and upon all the oaks of Bashan. In Psalm 28 (29) too it is sung: The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars; the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and will crush them like the calf of Lebanon (Ps 28 [29]:5, 6). And in Psalm 36 (37): I saw the wicked man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps 36 [37]:35, 36). The oaks of Bashan too, which Aquila translated δρύας, Symmachus and Theodotion βαλάνους, we know to be acorn-bearing trees, which, even if they bear fruit, are food for swine, not for men. Bashan is a region of Arabia, over which Og ruled, who was called king of Bashan; and it means αἰσχύνη, that is, ignominy; and if we chose to translate it confusion, that would rather signify σύγχυσιν, that is, Babylon, than Bashan. Upon all, then, who are lifted up in pride, and do works of ignominy, and wallow in the mire of lusts, the vengeance of the Lord will rise. But if the prudent reader should ask why cedar wood was set in the temple of the Lord, and why in Psalm 103 (104), according to the Hebrew truth, we read, The trees of the Lord shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which you have planted; there the sparrows will build their nests (Ps 103 [104]:16, 17); and why among the other trees the cedars too are summoned to the praises of the Lord; and why at the coming of the Savior, when all the trees and the wood of the field will clap with their branches, it is written: I will set in the waterless land the cedar and the box, and the cypress and the pine (Isa 41:19 LXX); and now the prophetic word threatens the day of the Lord upon the cedars of Lebanon? it must be said that out of the same kind of men some are raised up to the kingdom, others dragged down to punishment; and the cedars of Lebanon, which will be broken because of their pride, are chosen when they are of good odor and have said with the Apostle: We are the good odor of Christ (2 Cor 2:15).

Here he places the subtraction of things which make for defense. And first, as to things that pertain to preparing machines of war: either because of their height, and thus he says, "upon all the cedars"; or because of their strength, and thus he says, "upon all the oaks": "open your gates, O Libanus, and let fire devour your cedars" (Zech 11:1); and below this: "howl, you oaks of Basan, because the fenced forest is cut down" (Zech 11:2).

And upon all the lofty mountains, and upon all the hills that are lifted up. Just as in a good sense, according to the variety of virtues, men are called mountains and hills, so among the impious, according to the diversity of vices, and above all of pride, some are mountains, others hills, upon which the day of the Lord will be; of whom it is written in Ezekiel: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the mountains and the hills: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and your high places shall be scattered, and your altars shall be broken, and the rest (Ezek 6:3).

As to things which pertain to the fortification of places from nature: "and upon all the high mountains": "thus says the Lord God to the mountains, and to the hills, and to the rocks, and the valleys" (Ezek 6:3).

And upon every lofty tower, and upon every fortified wall. Those who refer these things to the times of Vespasian and Hadrian say that what is written was fulfilled bodily: that no lofty tower, no strongest wall, no multitude of ships and industry of trade could prevail against the might of the Roman army; but that the inhabitants of Judea came into such terror that they, with their wives and children, buried themselves in pits of the earth with the gold and silver which they thought would be a help to them, and sought out the deepest caves. For if the belly is the god of the gluttonous and the luxurious, why should not gold and silver be called the god of the avaricious? Others refer these things to Babylonian times. So I will run through each point according to the laws of tropology. A tower is built either for the defense of a city or for a lookout, so that the enemy may be seen coming from afar. Each of us, then, ought to build a tower, having first reckoned the cost, lest, according to the parable of the Gospel (Luke 14), he be laughed at when he cannot finish the work. This tower, well built, stands firm. But if, raised up in pride, it has no firm foundations, it will fall upon him by whom it was built, like that one in Siloam which killed eighteen men. Hence the Lord too says to his hearers: And unless you repent, you will likewise perish (Luke 13:3). In what follows too we shall read that the Lord built a tower in his vineyard, and made a winepress, and put a wall around it, but that all these things were destroyed and laid waste because they swelled with the vain brow of pride (Isa 5). Lofty walls too are built so that the city may not be quickly destroyed, so that it may not lie open to enemies: for the Churches are surrounded with the wisest men and fortified with every reason, lest any perverse doctrine prevail against the truth. Of such walls God speaks to Jerusalem: Behold, upon my hands I have painted your walls, and they are always in my sight (below, Isa 49:16 LXX). But if those who before had attacked the Church, having come to know the truth, pass over to the faith and fight for that which they had before attacked, then this will be fulfilled: You shall quickly be built by those by whom you had been destroyed (ibid., 17). In Leviticus too we read that a house which is in walled cities, if it has not been redeemed within the year, is confirmed to the buyer as a perpetual possession; but if it is in country places and villages which have no walls, it can always be redeemed, and the buyer's price remains unsettled (Lev 25).

As to things which pertain to the fortification of places from art: "and upon every high tower": "a day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high bulwarks. And I will distress men" (Zeph 1:16–17).

And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all that is beautiful to see. For Tarshish, which all translated alike, the Seventy alone translated sea. The Hebrews think that in their own tongue the sea is properly called THARSIS (תרסים), and that when it is called IAM (ים), it is called so not in the Hebrew tongue but in the Syriac. Jehoshaphat too had ships which he sent to Tarshish (1 Kgs 22:49), but they were broken at Ezion-geber. Solomon too had ships which went to Tarshish (1 Kgs 10:22) and returned after three years and brought the king silver and gold, ivory and apes. But because both kings had sinned, the one given to pleasure and a lover of women of foreign nations, the other joining himself with the king of Samaria, both of which things are referred to the pagans and the heretics, in whom there is nothing but the glitter of eloquence, and a sense built up by diabolical art, and dead speech, which is interpreted in the ivory teeth, and a likeness of human reason, which is perceived in the apes; therefore we read in the Psalms, With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish (Ps 47 [48]:8). And of these ships the same Isaiah speaks: Woe to the wings of the ships which are beyond Ethiopia (below, Isa 18:1 LXX). But there are on the contrary good ships too, of which it is said in the same psalms: Those who go down to the sea in ships and do business in many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep (Ps 106 [107]:23). For those who are not idle in the waves of this world, but work, and carry the Lord's merchandise, and hasten to come to the harbor of rest, they see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep, when they have come to deep knowledge and, searching all things, that is, even the deep things of God, have beheld his wonders. Josephus thinks Tarshish is Tarsus, a city of Cilicia; others think it a region of India, and that by this name too one of the twelve gems is called, the stone which among us is called chrysolite, from the likeness of its color to the sea. But it is better to take Tarshish absolutely as either the sea or the open main. For Jonah, sailing from Joppa, could not reach India, to which one cannot sail by that sea; but simply go out to the open sea and make for whatever islands. And what follows, And upon all that is beautiful to see, or, as the Seventy translated, And upon every sight of the beauty of ships, is to be taken in the same sense: that whatever seems beautiful in words and is built up by human reason will be destroyed by the day of the Lord, if it lifts itself up against the knowledge of God.

As to things which pertain to abundance of provisions, and thus he says: "and upon all the ships," in which provisions are borne, "of Tharsis," that is, of the sea, below: "howl, you ships of the sea, for the house is destroyed, from whence they were wont to come" (Isa 23:1).

"And upon all that is fair to behold": this pertains to the placating of enemies, or the increase of fighters: "who can despise the people of the Hebrews, who have such beautiful women?" (Jdt 10:18).

And the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the height of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day, and the idols shall be utterly broken. Human speech seems to have reason so long as it has not been compared with divine knowledge. But when falsehood draws near to the truth, like stubble to fire, it is quickly devoured and perishes, and all the doctrines of falsehood, which are now called idols because they are feigned and fabricated, will be utterly broken.

Here it is as if he concludes the proposition; and it is entirely the same as what was said before, except that something is added about the destruction of idols, so that he alone may be shown to be the highest.
"And idols shall be utterly destroyed": "your idols shall be broken in pieces and shall be no more, and your temples shall be destroyed" (Ezek 6:6).

The Creator ought to be known even by the light of nature, for he may be understood from his works and may thereby become the object of a more widely spread knowledge. To him, therefore, does it appertain to punish such as do not know God, for none ought to be ignorant of him. In the apostle's phrase, "From the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power," he uses the words of Isaiah, who for that same reason attests the very same Lord as arising "to shake terribly the earth."

Here he places the precaution of hiding; and it is the same as before, except that here it is foretold as in the future, because he had also explained by foretelling and not by calling down that their power was to be thrown down; "they shall go into the lower parts of the earth: they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be the portions of foxes" (Ps 63:9–10).

In that day man shall cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which he had made for himself, to worship moles and bats; and he shall go into the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth. We have often said that silver and gold are taken for speech and sense; and though these were given by God to men so that they might either speak of God or perceive God and praise their creator, they abuse this gift for the fashioning of idols; according to what is written: I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal of my silver and gold (Hos 2:8). When, then, someone, terrified by the fear of the Lord, has first hidden his idols in the cave of his breast and concealed them in the abysses of the earth, not daring to bring out what he had wickedly fashioned, the second advance is that he cast away what he had first concealed and not suffer it to be in him. For moles, as we have translated, the Seventy have vain things, Aquila ὀρυκτὰ, Symmachus unfruitful things; Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, PHARPHAROTH (פרפרות). It is an animal without eyes, which always digs the earth and throws out the soil, and, eating the roots underneath, is harmful to crops; the Greeks call it ἀσπάλακα. The bat, a bird of the night, which received from them the fitting name νυκτερὶς because it flits about in the night, is a small animal, like a mouse, sounding not so much with voice and song as with squeaking; and though it is seen to fly, it shuns the light and cannot bear to see the sun. To such animals are compared the idols, which, blind and dark, are worshiped by the blind, and all doctrines contrary to the truth.

Here he removes the third, namely confidence in idols. And first, he takes away their help; "to adore": "And I went in and saw, and behold every form of creeping things, and of living creatures, the abominations, and all the idols of the house of Israel, were painted" (Ezek 8:10). Below: "in that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which your hands have made for you to sin" (Isa 31:7).

And when these have been abandoned in the day of the Lord, those who have cast them away will enter the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones, so as to dwell not in the dust of the earth and in vile mud but in firm reason, and find for themselves the various openings of the virtues, through which they may be able to come to the truth. These things, according to the anagogy, I have touched on as I could in brief words; the Hebrews refer them to Babylonian times and the overthrow of Jerusalem, when the Lord rose to strike the land of the Jews.

Second, he returns to the protection of hiding, where it says, "and he shall go into the clefts of rocks": "every bondman and every freeman hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of mountains" (Rev 6:15).

Cease, therefore, from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he himself is reckoned lofty. The Seventy omitted this, and in the Greek copies it was added by Origen under asterisks from the edition of Aquila; in the Hebrew it reads thus: HEDALU LACHEM MEN AADAM ASER NASAMA BAAPHPHO CHI BAMA NESAB HU. Where we have said, he himself is reckoned lofty, Aquila translated, in what is this one reckoned. The Hebrew word BAMA (במה) means either ὕψωμα, that is, a high place, which we read both in the books of Kingdoms and in Ezekiel, or else in what, and it is written with the same letters, BETH, MEM, HE; and according to the character of the passages, if we wish to read in what, we say BAMMA; but if high place or lofty, we read BAMA. The Jews, then, understanding that the prophecy is about Christ, interpreted the ambiguous word in the worse sense, so that they might seem not to praise Christ but to count him as nothing. For what consequence of words is there, and what order of reason and sense, that we should say: Since these things are so, and the day of the Lord is to come, in which the whole state of Judea is to be overthrown and all things broken, I warn and command you to cease from the man who breathes and lives as we men do, because he is to be reckoned as nothing? Would any man so praise someone as to say: Beware of offending him who is altogether nothing? Therefore it must be understood the other way: Since all these things are to come upon you, and are foretold by the prophetic spirit, I warn and command you to cease from him who according to the flesh is indeed a man, and has a soul, and so breathes and draws breath through his nostrils as we men breathe and live, but who according to the divine majesty both is lofty and is reckoned and believed so. Turning it over silently in my mind, I cannot find the reason why the Seventy would not translate into Greek so clear a prophecy about Christ. For as to the others, who did translate it but dragged the ambiguous word to an impious sense, it is no wonder why they translated badly and would not say anything glorious about Christ, in whom they did not believe: being, namely, Jews or half-Jews, that is, Ebionites. And that Christ is lofty or most high, which among the Hebrews is called by another word, ELION (עליון), we read in Psalm 86 (87): Shall not a man say to Zion, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her (Ps 86 [87]:5)? And in the Gospel: And you, child, shall be called the Prophet of the Most High (Luke 1:76). And not to draw out a long rope (for in the exposition of the holy Scriptures we ought to follow the truth, not contention), in this place BAMA among the Hebrews means not lofty but a high place, that is, loftiness itself and sublimity: as if we were to say of someone, he is not divine but divination, not a stream but a fountain, not a man but humanity itself. Origen interpreted this passage thus: Because it is said in the singular of one man, it can be referred also to the Lord Savior, the Prophet commanding them to cease from him who is reckoned as something great, although at present he appears as a man and to have breath in his nostrils, as other men too breathe.

Here he places sound counsel for escape; therefore since all these things do not avail you, "cease therefore from the man," that is, cease from what is offensive to him, namely Christ, "whose breath is in his nostrils," that is, who breathes with his nostrils and lives like other men as to his humanity; "for he is reputed high," as to his divinity, by the saints and angels: "the Lord is high above all nations; and his glory above all the heavens" (Ps 113:4).

Or otherwise: it speaks of God in likeness to man through an anthropopathic figure: "from the man," that is, from God, "whose breath is in his nostrils"; this speaks in likeness to an angry man, who because of the multiplication of his breaths, breathes out through his nostrils; hence Homer says that strong men breathed out harsh power through each of their nostrils. "At the blast of the breath of your wrath" (Ps 18:15). Below: "his wrath burns, and is heavy to bear" (Isa 30:27), and again: "his breath as a torrent overflowing even to the midst of the neck, to destroy the nations unto nothing" (Isa 30:28). And this refers to the first, in which he takes away presumption of the mercy of God. "For he is reputed high," separately, as if alone, against the second.
3: Consider whether what follows in the prophet has not received its fulfillment: "The Lord of hosts has taken away from Judah and from Jerusalem, among other things, both the prophet and the wise craftsman"; that is, his Holy Spirit, who builds the church, which is indeed the temple, and household and city of God.… And so in this manner the law and the prophets were until John, but the dews of divine grace were withdrawn from the nation.

For behold, the ruler, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty and the strong: all the strength of bread, and all the strength of water. Up to this point they think it is spoken of the judgment. What follows concerns the captivity to come, which some refer to the Babylonians, others to the Romans. But it is better, as we said above, for everything to be referred to the Lord's passion. For after he was slain, all graces and gifts were taken away from the Jews, according to what is written in the Gospel: The Law and the Prophets until John the Baptist (Matt 11:13). And the order is this: Because you would not cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, who has been reckoned exalted, but on the contrary you shed the blood of the righteous one and devised the worst counsel, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is useless to us (Wis 2:12), therefore you shall eat the fruit of your own devices. Among the Jews after the Passion of the Lord nothing is strong, nothing is mighty, but all things are weak and languid. Nor can anyone among them say: I can do all things in him who strengthens me (Phil 4:13), Christ Jesus our Lord. And since according to the Seventy we read the mighty man and the mighty woman, to the mighty man we can fit this: Until we all meet in the perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph 4:13). And further, of the mighty woman: I wish, he says, to present you all as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor 11:2). Now the strength of bread and the strength of water is taken for all food and drink. We read that Moses was on Mount Sinai, and for forty days did not eat bread and did not drink water (Exod 34). That too which is said to Adam: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken (Gen 3:19), is to be heard in the same way. So also what is said by the Savior: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that goes forth through the mouth of God (Matt 4:4). The strength of bread, then, will be taken away from them: he who says, I am the living bread, who came down from heaven (John 6:51). And the strength of water, of which the same Lord spoke: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life (John 4:13). Of such loaves we read in Proverbs as well: Open your eyes, and be filled with loaves (Prov 20:13). The Jews have bread, but without strength; they have waters, but without vigor. For they read the Scriptures, but do not understand them; they hold the parchments, and have lost Christ, who is written in the parchments (1 Cor 3). For they are fed on milk, like little children, and not on solid food. And because they have lost their strength and are weak, therefore they eat vegetables. But the food of athletes is solid, which both sustains human life and furnishes strength to the living (Rom 14). Of such bread and water, that they are to be taken away from the Jews, another Prophet too bears witness, saying: Behold, the day will come, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the Lord (Amos 8:11).

The strong man and the man of war, the judge and the Prophet, and the soothsayer, and the old man. For strong man, which alone is in the Hebrew, the Seventy translated two words together, giant and strong man, meaning the same man to be the giant who is the strong man. Of the strong man we have spoken above. Now a giant in the good sense, that is, of the Lord and Savior, we read in the eighteenth psalm: He has exulted as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit even to its height (Ps 18 [19]:8). But if we read of Nimrod the giant (Gen 10), who was a hunter before the Lord, and of the giants (Gen 6) on whose account the flood came upon the earth, they are to be taken in the contrary sense. The man of war, too, we understand according to the history in this way: that they have been taken captive, and to this day are in servitude, and have not laid aside the yoke of slavery; that they do not even have judges of their own, but are subject to Roman judges, so much so that Roman rulers judge those of their princes who seem to be of standing among the people. But this too must be said: that there is no man of war among them in the Law, having the knowledge of judging, but all things are vain and perishable and full of folly. As for the Prophet, that he has ceased to exist among them no one doubts. We ask, according to the Hebrew, how we are to interpret soothsayer, whom all have translated diviner, except the Seventy, who for this translated conjecturer. And it must be said that future things are often told even through soothsayers, as we read of the diviner Balaam, and of the diviners of the five cities of the Philistines, Gaza and Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron and Ashdod, who give counsel how the ark of the Lord is to be sent back (1 Sam 6). And the sense is: both true things and false will alike be taken away from the Jews. The old man too, whom the Seventy translated elder, he understands to be taken away from the Jews, he who would know that in the holy Scriptures elders are chosen for merit and wisdom, not for age. For old men have not ceased to exist among the Jews; we often see them reach a decrepit old age. And we read in the beginning of Daniel, according to Theodotion, of two elders grown old in evil days (Dan 13). For Moses too is commanded to choose elders whom he knows to be elders (Exod 18). And the apostle Paul writes most fully to Timothy what kind of elder ought to be chosen (1 Tim 5). Hence it is said in Proverbs as well: The glory of old men is gray hair (Prov 20:29). What is this gray hair? Doubtless wisdom, of which it is written: Prudence is the gray hair of men (Wis 4:8). And though we read that from Adam to Abraham men lived nine hundred years and more (Gen 24), no one before was called an elder, that is, an old man, except Abraham, who is shown to have lived far fewer years. Hence John too, after the children and the young men, writes also to the old, saying: I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning (1 John 2:13). And Rehoboam the son of Solomon lost the kingdom for this reason, that he would not listen to the elders (1 Kgs 12).

Second, power consists in constancy of heart, and thus he says, the strong man, as far as it comes from the strength which is a power of the soul.

Third, it consists in the exercise of the art of war, and thus he says, the man of war.

99. Wisdom is required for the exercise of judgment: because of which Solomon asked for wisdom from God: give therefore to your servant an understanding heart . . . to discern between good and evil (1 Kgs 3:9).

And this may be had in three ways: either by human institution; and as to this he says, the judge, as it were, the expert in the law; or by divine inspiration, and as to this he says, the prophet; or by the revelation of a demon, and as to this he says, the diviner, because they divined on the altars of demons, and they sometimes spoke truths.

100. Authority is necessary for reverence, and this also consists in three things:

in dignity of office, and as to this he says, the prince; and by these he understands all other princes, as the Gloss says;

in uprightness of morals: the ancient in morals;

in maturity of countenance: the honorable in countenance.

Concerning this chapter, we first consider where it says, the diviner (Isa 3:2).

According to this it seems that it may be lawful to inquire into future things by diviners: for taking away something unlawful is not a punishment, but rather a benefit.

Moreover, the same thing seems to follow from the Gloss, which says diviners sometimes speak truths; but truth is to be received from wherever it comes, therefore it should also be received from diviners.

Moreover, since demons are clearest mirrors according to intellect, as Dionysius says, it seems that, at least in things that pertain to knowledge, it may not be evil to receive from them, and it will be lawful to turn thus to divination, and especially since no knowledge is evil, and divination may relate knowledge.

129. To this is to be said that divination, by its name, signifies a usurpation of a divine act, and this especially in the knowledge of future things which cannot be known naturally.

For there are certain future things which have determinate causes in nature, from which they arise necessarily, like an eclipse of the sun; and divination does not concern these things.

Other things also have determinate causes, from which they arise, as in many things, like drought in the dog days of summer; hence, divination does not concern these things (for such are the prognoses of doctors concerning health or death, and of mariners concerning a coming storm), unless perhaps they are foretold as if coming in immovable truth, for this belongs only to God.

There are also certain future things which do not have determinate causes in nature, and especially those which come to be from free will; and of these causes no one has foreknowledge except God, to whom all things are present because of the stability of his eternity, or someone who learns them from God. And if indeed such things are predicted by divine inspiration, it is prophecy, not divination; if, however, someone predicts by his own devising, deceptively, for the sake of some profit, as little old women do, it is called divination; and it is a sin, because it is a lie, since they assert uncertainties as true, and because it is deception, and because it is a usurpation of divinity.

130. Similarly, a prediction is called divination if it comes to be in any way whatsoever from the counsel of demons, who indeed are able to predict some future things, either because they themselves are the causes of them, or because they themselves know them through the revelation of good angels, or because they foreknow by natural knowledge in those things which have determinate causes in nature that are hidden from us and known to them because of the perspicacity of their intelligence and because of their long experience.

And nevertheless it is always a sin to inquire from them, and apostasy from faith, as Augustine says. And this is so for three reasons: first, because, although they may speak truths, nevertheless their intention is always to deceive; second, because they are not able to have certain knowledge, except of those things which they know through revelation; third, because we are not able to be at the same time sharers in the gifts of God and of the devil; and among all these, this last reason is foremost. And although it may be a benefit simply, nevertheless it is a punishment to those who follow such things, because it is contrary to their will.

The captain of fifty. Συνεκδοχικῶς, the whole from a part. For just as those who command a hundred soldiers are called Centurions, and those who command a thousand Chiliarchs, whom we call Tribunes, from the fact that they command a tribe: so in the army of Israel those who were at the head of fifty soldiers were called captains of fifty. Hence too we call Decurions those who command ten men. Nor is it a wonder if among the Jews every rank of warriors has perished, since they have no power to serve under the sword and to bear arms. But since the number fifty is always referred to penitence, and Christ is the prince of penitence and the head of those who are saved through penitence, let us briefly lay open the mysteries of this number. In Genesis we read, when Abraham speaks to the Lord, that he said first that the city should be saved for fifty righteous, if they were found in it. And in Numbers there is the most celebrated festival of the seven weeks, that is, of Pentecost. The Jubilee too, that is, the year of remission, which is woven of seven weeks of years, that is, of forty-nine years, in which the trumpets sound and the ancient possession returns to everyone, contains this mystery. Hence David too writes the Psalm of penitence at the fiftieth number. We read also in the same book of Numbers that of the booty and spoils the priests were to receive the fiftieth head, of men as well as of beasts, and the Levites who guard the doors of the tabernacle the fiftieth. That parable of the Gospel as well (Luke 7 and 16), in which two debtors are spoken of, one who owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty, refers to this understanding. Hence the Apostle too, among the Ephesians, to whom he had unfolded every mystical thing, wishes to remain until Pentecost, until they should be perfectly converted to the Lord, saying: For a great and evident door has been opened to me, but there are many adversaries (1 Cor 16:9). But the devil also imitates the army of Israel, concerning which Jethro had given counsel to his son-in-law Moses, that he should set over the people tribunes and centurions and captains of fifty (Exod 18). Hence the impious king (2 Kgs 1) sends two captains of fifty with the soldiers under them to bring Elijah: they were consumed by divine fire. But the third of them is saved, who, having turned to prayers, had come to know the mysteries of penitence. Hence the Jews too, unwilling that the Lord should be perfect or the captain of fifty, say to him: You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham? (John 8:57). And he, knowing himself to be the prince not only of the penitent but also of the righteous, answered: Before Abraham was, I am (ibid., 58). And that the Lord is the Captain of Fifty we can understand from a single festival, of which he says: The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath (Matt 12:8). If of the Sabbath, then of the Kalends too. If of the Kalends, then of the Pasch, that is, of the Unleavened Bread. If of the Pasch, then of the Jubilee. If of the Jubilee, then of Tabernacles. If of Tabernacles, then of Pentecost, which is referred to the fiftieth number.

And the honorable in countenance, and the counselor. For two, that is, honorable in countenance, and counselor, the Seventy translated one, wonderful man counselor. Among the other graces the Lord will take this too away from Judea, that they have no counselor, but do everything without counsel. And there is that praiseworthy and admirable saying of a Greek poet: "He is first in happiness who is wise of himself; second, he who listens to the wise." But he who lacks both is useless, both to himself and to all. Hence we read this too in our books: Let your friends be very many, but your counselor one of a thousand (Sir 6:6). And again: Do all things with counsel (Prov 13:10); and prudence will give you a wonderful counselor. Decrees of the Senate too are called consulta, and the chief men of Rome were once called consuls, either from consulting for the citizens or from ruling all things by counsel. And we in the Church have our senate, the assembly of elders. Since, then, among other things Judea has lost even its old men, how will it be able to have counsel, which properly belongs to the elders?

And the wise architect. For which Aquila translated the wisest of craftsmen, to show that they once had many craftsmen: such as was that Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, whom God filled with the spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge, so that in every work he was a most accomplished workman, not only in gold and silver but also in bronze and the other things that Moses enumerates, he who built the Tabernacle of God (Exod 31). Since, then, they have lost their architects, all the grace of building has been transferred to the Church. Hence the apostle Paul says: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation (1 Cor 3:10). Jeremiah too was an architect, who not only rooted up and dug under and destroyed, but also built (Jer 18). Hence the same Apostle says: We are God's husbandry, God's building (1 Cor 3:9). Our Lord too is called the builder of walls (Eph 2). And in the Gospel he who made all things is taunted as the son of a carpenter (Matt 13). In the volume of Kings too we read that king Solomon sent and took Hiram the Tyrian, the son of a widow woman, who was of the tribe of Naphtali and had a Tyrian father, a worker in bronze. And he came in to the king and did all the works for king Solomon: in him there is a type of the Church to be built, which was begotten not only of the tribe of Judah but also of Naphtali, and of a Tyrian father, he who had a widowed mother, because she had lost her former husband (1 Kgs 7). And many more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband (Isa 54). But in the book of Chronicles too we read of the valley of craftsmen: And Seraiah begot Joab, the father of the valley of craftsmen: for craftsmen were there (1 Chr 4:14). They are said to dwell in a valley for this reason, that knowledge did not puff them up, but they followed the humble and meek Jesus, and could say with the Apostle: For I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an Apostle (1 Cor 15:9). And elsewhere: We know in part, and we prophesy in part, and now we see through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor 13:9).

And the one prudent in mystic speech. For which the Seventy translated the prudent hearer; Theodotion, the prudent enchanter; Aquila, the prudent whisperer; Symmachus, the one prudent in mystic speech, whom we too have followed in this place. First it must be said, according to the Seventy, that among the other spiritual graces a prudent hearer too is necessary in the Church. For to one is given prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits (1 Cor 12:10). Hence there were also established among the people of the Jews priestly ranks, to discern prophets and false prophets, that is, to understand who spoke from the Spirit of God and who from the contrary spirit. Let us read Jeremiah. But the prudent one in mystic speech (Jer 14), or the whisperer, and, as Theodotion would have it, the enchanter, seems to me to be a man learned and practiced both in the Law and the Prophets and in the Gospel and the Apostles, who can heal each disturbance of the soul by his teaching and bring it back to a settled state of mind: while the fornicator recovers chastity, and the glutton frugality, and the man once greedy gives alms. Sift through all the synagogues of the Jews, and you will be able to find no teacher who enjoins holy things and, despising riches, teaches that poverty is to be pursued. Of such enchanters against serpents and asps, that is, against sinners who have abandoned the righteousness of God, David spoke in the Psalm: Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly, they have spoken falsehoods. Their fury is after the likeness of a serpent: like the deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of the enchanters, nor of the sorcerer who charms wisely (Ps 57 [58]:4ff.). Every word of the Apostle is an enchantment against serpents and asps, which sinners and heretics do not hear, because they shut their ears so as not to hear the truth.

101. Some princes are useful for the government of the people, or for dealing with doubtful affairs, and as to this he says, and the counsellor; or for constructing buildings: the architect, which comes from archos, which means "prince," and techne, which means "art," especially mechanical art. The architect is said to be the principal artist, who directs the other artists to introduce the form and prepare the matter, according to the consideration of the end, which he has knowledge of in use or reason.

102. But wisdom, according to the Philosopher, is said to be twofold: namely, universal and particular.

In defining particular wisdom, he says that it is the virtue through which man is placed in the utmost of any art, such as medicine, and that doctor is called wise who is most certain in things that pertain to medicine; and a builder is called wise similarly, and thus for others. And it is in this way that it is understood here.

Universal wisdom is that which is the utmost in all arts and sciences, and it is by this that man is raised to knowledge of the noblest things, that is, of separated, or spiritual, substances; and this, according to the Philosopher, is metaphysics, and, according to us, is theology.

103. Third, someone is necessary for teaching divine things, and as to this, he says: and the skillful in mystical speech; "mystical" comes from mystim, which means "secret," that is, pertaining to divine words which are secret. And concerning all these things it is stated in 2 Kings 24:15 that they were carried away by Nebuchadnezzar into Babylon: and he carried away Joachin into Babylon, and the king's mother, and the king's wives, and his eunuchs: and the judges of the land he carried into captivity.

And I will give children to be their princes. If it is said in the person of the Prophet: For behold, the ruler, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty man and the mighty woman: all the strength of bread, and all the strength of water, and the rest, how does the same prophet now say: I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them? Therefore, according to prophetic custom, while the Prophet is speaking, God suddenly speaks through the Prophet in his own person, and says: I will give children to be their princes: for having removed the things I had given before, and having taken away good things as though in anger, now on the contrary I will give evil things. I took away the old man and the captain of fifty, and the wonderful counselor, and the wise architect, and the prudent hearer, and so on. In their place I will give children as princes. For those who have lost the elder, such as the discourse above has shown, such as Abraham too was who was first called an elder, rightly receive young men as princes (Gen 7). Of these we read in Ecclesiastes too: Woe to you, O city, whose king is a youth, and your princes eat in the morning. Blessed is the land whose king is a son of the freeborn (Eccl 10:16). Such a young king was Rehoboam the son of Solomon, who followed the counsels of the young men (1 Kgs 12): not that he was young in age, but in wisdom. Otherwise, he is related to have received the kingdom at forty years and more. And on the contrary, Solomon was twelve years old when he took up the rule, and because he had wisdom, he was therefore not called a youth. For there was in him breadth of heart and amplitude of wisdom as great as the sand on the shores of the sea. Hence the Apostle too writes to Timothy: Let no one despise your youth (1 Tim 4:12). For he who is young in age is an old man in maturity. And Daniel, according to Theodotion, was called a boy before he judged (Dan 13); but after God stirred up his spirit in him and he judged the elders, he received the dignity of the eldership. To Jeremiah too, who had said to the Lord who was sending him, You who are ruler, O Lord: Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a youth (Jer 1:6), the Lord answered: Do not say, I am a youth; for before you were formed in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from your mother's womb I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet among the nations. For this reason, I think, the young widows too are commanded by the Apostle (1 Tim 5) to take husbands and be mothers of families and bring up their children, because many have gone back after Satan; and when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation, because they have made void their first faith. Nor is a widow supported on the Church's provisions unless she is sixty years old and has maturity of character as well as of age. One might think that what the Apostle forbids (1 Tim 3), that a neophyte be made a bishop, pertains to this, because he is a little one in faith, lest, puffed up into pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. And the judgment of the devil is nothing else but pride, on account of which he fell from heaven. Hence the Savior too says: I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18).

And the effeminate shall rule over them. For which in the Hebrew is written THALULIM (תעלולים), whom the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted as mockers, Aquila ἐναλλάκτας, those who change themselves and take turns in shameful acts, such as we read of in the book of Judges concerning the Levite's concubine in Gibeah (Judg 19). Let us consider the Patriarchs of the Jews, and the young men or boys, effeminate and abounding in luxuries, and we shall see that the prophecy has been fulfilled. We may also call mockers the teachers of the people of Israel, who devour the people of God like a morsel of bread, and interpret the holy Scriptures perversely, and make sport of the folly of their disciples.

104. And I will give children. Here he shows the subversion of the government as to unworthy men being placed over them. And this is divided into two parts:

in the first is placed the authority of unworthy men;

in the second, the consequent disturbance of the people, where it says, and the people shall fall one upon another (Isa 3:5).

Now, they are unworthy as to lack of wisdom and of age, and thus he says I will give children to be their princes; and as to lack of virtue, and thus he says: and the effeminate shall rule over them, that is, the lustful and the weak: I will give you kings in my wrath (Hos 13:11).

And the people shall rush, man upon man, each one upon his neighbor: the boy shall riot against the old man, and the base against the noble. When the princes are young men, and mockers of the Lord, such as the prophetic discourse describes, then no order will be kept, whether of dignity or of age or of knowledge; but boys will rebel against old men, and the base against the noble, and they will fall upon one another. And that saying of the Apostle will be fulfilled: Biting one another, you have been consumed by one another (Gal 5:15). That these things befell the people of the Jews under Titus the son of Vespasian, Josephus writes (Jewish War, Book 5): and that, when they were being besieged by the Romans, Jerusalem was divided by sedition into three parts, and some held the citadel and the Temple, others the lower, others the upper part of the city.

105. The effect of the government in the disturbance of the people is touched on in three ways.

First, universal dissension, hence he says: the people shall fall, from the unity of peace through which they are a people, one to another, that is, one against another: where there is no governor, the people shall fall (Prov 11:14); they were led away as a flock: they shall be afflicted, because they have no shepherd (Zech 10:2).

Second, dissolution of friendship: every man to his neighbor, that is, against his neighbor: every brother will utterly supplant, and every friend will walk deceitfully (Jer 9:4).

Third, confusion of rank: the child shall make a tumult against the ancient, and the base against the honorable: they respected not the persons of the priests, neither had they pity on the ancient (Lam 4:16).

For a man shall take hold of his brother, of the household of his father: You have a garment, be our prince; and let this ruin be under your hand. For ruin, Symmachus and Theodotion translated weakness; the Seventy, food. It signifies the scarcity of men, and above all the want of all things, so that whoever has food and clothing is believed to be powerful and rich and illustrious. And what it says according to the Hebrew, And let this ruin be under your hand, has this sense: Let our misery and calamity be sustained and protected by your help. And this must be considered, that each man chooses for himself his own prince, and that there is sedition in the choosing of princes, while some think some men worthy of rule and others others. Nor do they say to them, Your possessions and riches and revenues will be able to sustain us; but, This weakness, or my food, will be healed by your judgment and will hang upon it.

106. Shall take hold. Here he shows the subversion of the government as to the refusal of office of those invited to rule, as if it were something ruinous. And this is divided into two parts:

in the first, the invitation of the electors is set out;

in the second, the refusal of the one elected, where it says, and in that day he shall answer (Isa 3:7).

Concerning the first, three things are set out, namely, the election itself, the occasion of the election, and the charge of office.

The election is irregular, because it is by only one; hence he says, there will be a tumult, for, that is, because, they did not elect in common; but a man shall take hold of his brother, that is, one joined by blood, one of the house of his father, that is, one accepted in familiarity, even though he is base: he that builds up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity (Mic 3:10). And this is against the form observed in Numbers 1 in the election of princes done by the precept of the Lord, the authority of the superior, and the consent of the multitude.

But the occasion is base, because it is on account of riches; hence he says: you have a garment, for he hopes for temporal assistance; and this is against the form handed on in Exodus 18:21–22: and provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, in whom there is truth, and that hate avarice, and appoint of them rulers of thousands, and of hundreds . . . who may judge the people at all times.

But the charge is dangerous; hence he says: be you our ruler, and let this ruin, that is, danger, be under your hand, that is, under your keeping and defense. Keep this man: and if he shall slip away, your life shall be for his life (1 Kgs 20:39).

And he will answer in that day, saying, I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor garment; do not appoint me prince of the people. For physician, Symmachus and the Seventy translated prince; Theodotion, ἐπιδεσμεύοντα, one who binds up wounds and provides for health. He will answer is not found in the Hebrew, but has been added from the Seventy. For in the Hebrew it is joined to what is written above: In that day he will say, I am not a physician, and the rest. And he will say it who has been chosen prince. And just as the people desires to have as prince the one whom it perceives to be richer in comparison with itself, so the one who is chosen, considering his poverty and his weakness, testifies that he is unworthy of the honor conferred and cannot heal vices, that is, cure the sick, give food to the hungry, clothe the naked, since he himself is scarcely able to sustain himself. Let us not, then, at once acquiesce in the judgment of the multitude; but when chosen for leadership, let us know our measure and be humbled under the mighty hand of God, because God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5). How many, having neither bread nor clothing, though they themselves are hungry and naked, and have no spiritual food and have not kept the tunic of Christ whole, promise others both nourishment and clothing, and, full of wounds, boast that they are physicians; nor do they keep that saying of Moses: Provide another whom you may send, and that other command: Seek not to be made a judge, lest perhaps you be unable to take away iniquities (Sir 7:6). Jesus alone heals all sicknesses and infirmities, of whom it is written: Who heals the broken in heart, and binds up their bruises (Ps 146 [147]:3).

107. He shall answer. Here the refusal of the one elected is set out.

And first, his reasonable excuse is shown;

second, his renunciation of office is concluded where it says, make me not ruler of the people.

In excuse, he brings forward three things, namely, his impotence to repel harmful things: I am no healer, namely, that I might heal your miseries: is there no balm in Galaad? Or is there no physician there? (Jer 8:22); to supply need: and in my house there is no bread, by which I might supply the need of your hunger: the little ones have asked for bread, and there was none to break it unto them (Lam 4:4); to foster or preserve what is necessary: nor clothing, by which heat is preserved: she shall not fear for her house in the cold of snow: for all her domestics are clothed with double garments (Prov 31:21).

108. Make me not ruler of the people. Here his renunciation of office is concluded, where a threefold reason is placed, namely, the impediment of devout contemplation: can I leave my fatness, which both gods and men make use of? (Judg 9:9); of sweet affection: can I leave my sweetness? (Judg 9:11); and of spiritual exultation: can I forsake my wine, that cheers God and men, and be promoted among the other trees? (Judg 9:13).

For Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed: because their tongue and their devices are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty. The recognition of their countenance has answered them: and they have proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and have not hidden it. It is the Prophet who says this, not, as many think, the one who had been chosen prince. And he says that no one is willing to be set over a sinful people for this reason, that both Judah and Jerusalem, both the city and the province of Judea, or the tribe of Judah, have fallen alike. And he gives the causes of their impiety: that they blasphemed against the Lord and said, Away, away, crucify such a one; we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15, 16), and by the fury of their tongue provoked the most merciful Lord to bitterness.

109. For Jerusalem is ruined. Here he sets out the cause of this renunciation.

And first, he sets out the proximate cause, namely, the punishment of universal ruin; hence is said on the part of the prophet: therefore he will refuse, for, that is, because, Jerusalem is ruined, that is, the city itself, and Judah, the province itself, is fallen, from its integrity through punishment, below: they have led away the strong ones thereof into captivity, they have destroyed the houses thereof, they have brought it to ruin (Isa 23:13).

110. Second, he sets out the remote cause, namely, their fault. And this is divided into three parts:

in the first part, he adds to the weight of the fault,

in the second, he ordains the punishment for the fault, where it says, woe to their souls (Isa 3:9);

in the third, he shows the justice of the one who punishes, where it says, say to the just man (Isa 3:10).

He adds to the weight of their sin from three things:

from the species of their sin, because it is blasphemy against God; hence he says: therefore it is fallen because their tongue is against the Lord, below: upon whom have you jested? Upon whom have you opened your mouth wide, and put out your tongue? (Isa 57:4).

Second, from the novelty of their sin; hence he says: their devices are against the Lord: their own devices now have beset them about, they have been done before my face (Hos 7:2).

The climax of your sin is that you hate the righteous one whom you killed, as well as those who by his grace are godly, righteous and loving. It is for this reason that the Lord said, "Woe to their soul, because they have taken evil counsel against themselves, saying, 'Let us take away the just one, for he is distasteful to us.' " Although you did not offer a sacrifice to Baal, like your ancestors, and did not offer cakes in groves and on hills to the heavenly army, you did not accept the Lord's Christ. Whoever does not know Christ does not know the will of God. Whoever rejects and hates him obviously rejects and hates the one who sent him. Whoever does not have faith in him does not believe the words of the prophets who preached his good news and proclaimed him to all people.

And the prophet himself at once supplies the reason, why he called them rulers of Sodom, and people of Gomorrah: "For your hands are full of blood." And again a little further on :

"They have proclaimed their sin as Sodom and made it manifest. Woe to their soul, because they have taken evil counsel with themselves, saying, We will bind the just, for he is burdensome to us."

Since he so very clearly mentions some one's blood, and a plot against some one just man, what could this be but the plot against our Saviour Jesus Christ, through which and after which all the things aforesaid overtook them?
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

The Jews in their imaginings, and in their agreeing to act unjustly against the Lord, forgot that they were bringing wrath upon themselves.
