Therefore does the Word lament for them, saying, ‘Why do the people exalt themselves, and the nations imagine vain things?’ For vain indeed was the imagination of the Jews, meditating death against the Life, and devising unreasonable things against the ‘Word of the Father.’ For who that looks upon their dispersion, and the desolation of their city, may not aptly say, ‘Woe unto them, for they have imagined an evil imagination, saying against their own soul, let us bind the righteous man, because he is not pleasing to us.’ And full well is it so, my brethren; for when they erred concerning the Scriptures, they knew not that ‘he who diggeth a pit for his neighbour falleth therein; and he who destroyeth a hedge, a serpent shall bite him.’ And if they had not turned their faces from the Lord, they would have feared what was written before in the divine Psalms: ‘The heathen are caught in the pit which they made; in the snare which they hid is their own foot taken. The Lord is known when executing judgments: by the works of his hands is the sinner taken.’ Let them observe this, and how that ‘the snare they know not shall come upon them, and the net they hid take them.’ But they understood not these things, for had they done so, ‘they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.’

They bound Jesus and led him to the meeting place of the high priest. Can you recognize that this was already written? Isaiah says, "Woe to their souls because they have taken evil counsel against themselves, saying, 'Let us bind the just one, for he is troublesome to us.' " Woe to their souls indeed! Let us see why. Isaiah was sawn in two, but afterwards the people were restored. Jeremiah was thrown into the dungeon, but the Jews had their wound healed. In these instances the sin was against a man, and therefore less. However, when they sinned not against a man but against God become human, then woe to their souls!

It is the tribes, then, that are meant by the names of the patriarchs. From the tribe of Simeon come the scribes, from that of Levi the chief priests, who brought their wickedness to completion and filled up the entire measure of their fathers' ungodliness in the passion of the Lord. They took counsel against the Lord Jesus, to kill him, even as Isaiah says, "Alas for their souls! Because they have devised an evil counsel against themselves, saying. 'Let us bind the just one, for he is profitless to us.' " They killed the prophets and apostles who announced the coming of the Lord of salvation and preached his glorious passion and resurrection. Thereafter, in their greed and out of their desire for earthly wickedness, they fled from sharing in the divine, from chastity of body and moderation of spirit, contempt for money and profit in grace.
On the Blessings of the Patriarchs 3.13

For he [Jesus] had done so many good works among them. He had given sight to the blind, feet to the lame, the power of walking to the palsied, life also to the dead; for all these good works they paid him death as his price, appraised at thirty pieces of silver. It is related also in the Gospels that he was bound. This also the word of prophecy had foretold by Isaiah, saying, "Woe to their soul, who have devised a most evil device against themselves, saying, 'Let us bind the just one, seeing that he is unprofitable to us.' "

Woe to their soul, because evils have been repaid to them. Say to the righteous that it is well, because they have eaten the fruit of their own devices. Woe to the wicked unto evil: for the reward of his hands shall be done to him. According to the Hebrew and the other Translators it has this sense: Woe to them, because they have received back their crimes. Therefore you who hear, or who read the book of the Prophet, praise the righteousness of God, because he has done well: because the wicked have eaten the labors of their own hands. And woe to the wicked people unto evil: for it has received what it deserved. And he who handed over his prince to the Roman power himself lies subject to Roman servitude. But according to the Seventy Translators, who said: Woe to their soul, because they have devised the worst counsel against themselves, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, because he is useless to us; therefore they shall eat the fruits of their works, it is clearly said of the passion of Christ, that they entered upon the worst counsel, not so much against the righteous one as against themselves and their own soul; and now they eat the fruits of their works. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap (Gal 6:5-8), and each one will bear his own burden.

The recognition of their countenance will answer them: that is, they have received back their own sins; or, as the Seventy translated, the confusion of their countenance has stood against them: that is, they have always had their own offenses before their eyes. And just as the Sodomites, sinning with all license and having not even any shame in their crime, said to Lot, Bring the men out, that we may lie with them (Gen 19:5): so these too, crying out publicly, proclaimed their sin and had no modesty in blaspheming. For to hide one's impiety is the second plank after shipwreck and a consolation of miseries. Hence they are also called princes of Sodom, because they had the sins of Sodom.

Again, they are to be admonished that if they are not afraid of being wicked; they should at least be ashamed of being seen for what they are. Often a sin that is concealed is avoided, because a mind that is ashamed to be taken for what it does not fear to be in fact is sometimes ashamed to be in fact what it avoids appearing to be. On the other hand, when a person is shamelessly and notoriously wicked, then, the more freely he commits every kind of evil, the more he thinks it lawful, and in imagining it lawful, he is thereby without doubt immersed in it all the more. Therefore, it is written, "They have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom, and they have not hid it." For if Sodom had concealed its sin, it would still have sinned, but in fear. But it had completely lost the curb of fear, in that it did not seek even darkness in its sinning. Therefore, it is said again, "The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is multiplied." For sin in words is sin in act, but sin that is cried out is sin committed with deliberation.

Third, from the publication of their sin, whence he says: the show of their countenance, because by their countenance they make their sin to be shown to others; has answered them, in punishment as to their bearing; and as to the commendation of their sin, he says: and they have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom, that is, they have praised it: you had a harlot's forehead, you would not blush (Jer 3:3).

111. This is explained otherwise in the Gloss: the show of their countenance, that is, the knowledge of their sins, which they will have in their intellect, because the senses are in the countenance, has answered them, who ask why they are punished.

Or otherwise: the show of their countenance, that is, the remorse of conscience, has answered them, as punishment. And mystically, this refers to the sin of those who saw Christ and did not wish to know him, because of which their conscience reproves them, as the Gloss says. And because the justice of God does not allow such grave evils to be unpunished, therefore woe to their souls, not only to their bodies, for evils have been rendered to them, in the foreknowledge of God; or the past tense is used here for the future.

The aforesaid Scribes and Pharisees therefore placed James upon the pinnacle of the temple, and cried out to him and said: 'You just one, in whom we ought all to have confidence, forasmuch as the people are led astray after Jesus, the crucified one, declare to us, what is the gate of Jesus.'

And he answered with a loud voice, 'Why do you ask me concerning Jesus, the Son of Man? He himself sits in heaven at the right hand of the great Power, and is about to come upon the clouds of heaven.'

And when many were fully convinced and gloried in the testimony of James, and said, 'Hosanna to the Son of David,' these same Scribes and Pharisees said again to one another, 'We have done badly in supplying such testimony to Jesus. But let us go up and throw him down, in order that they may be afraid to believe him.'

And they cried out, saying, 'Oh! Oh! The just man is also in error.' And they fulfilled the Scripture written in Isaiah, 'Let us take away the just man, because he is troublesome to us: therefore they shall eat the fruit of their doings.' [Isaiah 3:10 LXX] 

So they went up and threw down the just man, and said to each other, 'Let us stone James the Just.' And they began to stone him, for he was not killed by the fall; but he turned and knelt down and said, 'I entreat you, Lord God our Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' [Luke 23:34]
Memoirs (Book V), as quoted in Church History (Book II), Chapter 23, Sections 13-15
(as quoted by Eusebius of Caesarea, AD 339)

112. And lest the punishment be supposed to envelop everyone, to this is added the justice of God in the separation of the good from the wicked; and concerning this, he does two things.

First, he places the recompense of the good, saying, say to the just man, to any just man, that it is well, it will be for him, when the others are condemned, for the fruit, that is, his reward, he shall eat of his devices, as if taking the fruit of his good inventions. For just as the wicked are solicitous to find ways to sin, so the good are solicitous to find how they might please God: he that is without a wife is solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord: how he may please God (1 Cor 7:32); for you shall eat the labors of your hands: blessed are you (Ps 127[128]:2).

115. It should be noted on verse 10 above, say to the just man that . . . he shall eat the fruit, that the fruit of the just man is:

first, that which he returns, and this is the fruit of his activity: you should bring forth fruit; and your fruit should remain (John 15:16); of his preaching: let us offer the sacrifice of praise always to God, that is to say, the fruit of lips confessing to his name (Heb 13:15); of his confession.

Second, that which he receives, and this is the fruit of remission of fault, below: the iniquity of the house of Jacob shall be forgiven: and this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away (Isa 27:9); of participation of grace: but the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy (Gal 5:22); of contemplation of wisdom: the purchasing thereof is better than the merchandise of silver, and her fruit than the chief and purest gold (Prov 3:14).

Third, that which he seeks: in the delight of the Lord: his fruit was sweet to my palate (Song 2:3); in the society of the heavenly choir: O mountains of Israel, shoot forth your branches, and yield your fruit to my people of Israel (Ezek 36:8); in the reception of the divine gift: your plants are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of the orchard (Song 4:13).

Second, he places the punishment of the wicked, saying, woe to the wicked unto evil, that is, for the evil which threatens them, the reward of his hands shall be given him: the sinner has been caught in the works of his own hands (Ps 9:17[16]).

As individuals we have our own officers, but the whole multitude is handed over to several, according to that which is written in Isaiah: "my people, your officers plunder you, and those who are powerful lord it over you" — the officers lord it over us, if we owe anything.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 35

But now, what wounds can the conquered show, what injuries to gaping vitals, what tortures of the limbs, when faith did not fail in combat but perfidy arrived before the combat? Nor does the necessity of the crime excuse the one who was caught, where the crime is of the will. I do not say this to burden the cases of the brothers but rather to stimulate the brothers to prayers of satisfaction. For since it is written, "They that call you blessed send you into error and destroy the way of your steps," one who consoles the sinner with flattering blandishments furnishes the means for sinning and does not check transgressions but nourishes them. But one who rebukes at the same time that he instructs with firmer counsels urges a brother on to salvation.

Isaiah also, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out and chides the daughters of Zion who have been defiled by gold and raiment, and he reproves those who have an abundance of harmful riches and withdraw from God for the sake of the pleasures of time.… This, God blames; this, he brands with reproach. By this he declares that they have been defiled; by this they have departed from the true adornment and have merited disgrace and shame. Having put on silk and purple, they cannot put on Christ; adorned with gold and pearls and necklaces, they have lost the adornments of the heart and soul. Who would not detest and shun what has caused another's ruin? Who would seek and take what has served as a sword and weapon for the death of another? If, on draining the cup, he who had taken the potion should die, you would know that what he drank was poison; if, after taking food, he who had taken it should perish, you would know that what could kill, when taken, was deadly. Seeing this you would not eat nor would you drink from that which had been used by those who died. Now what ignorance of the truth it is, what madness of mind to wish for what has always been and still is harmful, and to think that you yourself will not perish from the same causes from which you know that others have perished!
Treatise II. On the Dress of Virgins 13

Let us hearken to God, as he proclaims through Isaiah: "O my people, they that call you blessed lead you astray, throw you down headlong." Who is more guilty of throwing the people of God down headlong? He who relies on the power of the free will and scorns the help of the Creator and is secure in his own will, or he who fears the judgment of God at every thought of his precepts?

The Lord speaks by the mouth of Isaiah, saying, "O my people, they who call you happy cause you to err and destroy the way of your paths." How do you help me by telling my misdeeds to others? You may, without my knowing of it, hurt someone else by telling of my sins (or rather of those sins you slanderously attribute to me). While you are eager to spread the news everywhere, you may pretend to confide in individual people, giving them the impression that you have not talked to anyone else. This behavior is not intended to correct me but to indulge your own failings. The Lord commands that those who sin against us are to be approached privately or in the presence of a witness. If the one who is confronted continues in sin, then he or she is to be regarded as a heathen and a publican.

My people, their exactors have despoiled them, and women have ruled over them. For women, whom Symmachus alone translated so, and who in Hebrew are called NASIM (נשים), Aquila and the Seventy translated ἀπαιτοῦντας, which means exactors; Theodotion δανειστὰς, that is, usurers. Now the prophetic discourse speaks against the Scribes and Pharisees, who for the sake of base gain, to receive tithes and first-fruits, denied the Son of God. And he does not call them masters, scribes and teachers, but exactors (Luke 20), who think that piety is a means of gain, and devour, not, as in the Apostle, only the houses of widows, but the whole people; and, accusing their luxury and their shameful way of life, he calls them not only exactors, as men seen to exact money from the unwilling, but women, because they do everything for lust's sake and are given over to pleasures. Let us too, then, beware that we be not exactors among the people; that, as the impious Porphyry says, matrons and women be not our senate, ruling in the Churches, and that the favor of women judge not of the priestly rank.

My people, those who call you blessed, they deceive you, and scatter the way of your steps, or throw it into confusion. He had called the Scribes and Pharisees exactors, not masters; and above, mockers, who because of gifts, which blind the eyes even of the wise, not only did not rebuke the sinners among the people, but for the sake of riches and profits extolled them with praises, calling them blessed, and pillars of the house of God, and the other things flatterers are wont to say. He, then, is the churchman teacher who moves tears, not laughter, who rebukes sinners, who calls no one blessed, no one happy, and does not anticipate the sentence of his judge, since holy Scripture says (Sir 11:30): Call no man blessed before death. But in another place too we read (Prov 27:14): He who blesses his friend in the morning with a loud voice differs in nothing from one who curses. Therefore, despising the judgments of men, let us neither be lifted up by their praises nor saddened by their disparagements; but let us enter upon the right way and the paths trodden by the holy prophets, and let us hear the prophet Jeremiah saying: Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the everlasting paths of the Lord, which is the good way, and walk in it (Jer 6:16). And if ever we go astray and, being men, proceed by a perverse road, let us await the promises of the Lord, who says through Ezekiel: I will give them another way, and another heart (Ezek 36). But the exactors have perverted and troubled the way of the Lord, so that, having the key of knowledge, they neither entered themselves nor suffered the people to enter, but made them lose the way of the truth, which says in the Gospel: I am the way, and the life, and the truth (John 14:6).

Those who are zealous in the service of God, however, do not get a reward of praise, nor indeed do those who are concerned about the laws of God look for this return. For praise is often known to injure many, since it makes them less attuned and slows their pace. If a person thinks he has reached the goal of his endeavor—and praise gives him to understand that he has—he stops his race and victory eludes him. This was revealed by the God of the universe, speaking through the prophet: "My people, they that call you blessed, the same deceive you and destroy the way of your steps." For praise slackens the intensity of their zeal and prevents them from reaching the goal.

113. As for my people. Here the oppression of the people is denounced, in as far as it is the sin of the man who oppresses them, and this divided into two parts:

in the first, the vice of oppression is set out;

in the second, the judgment of punishment is introduced, where it says, the Lord stands up to judge (Isa 3:13).

Now, certain people were oppressing them in three ways.

First, princes were oppressing them by pillaging them through violence, and as to this he says, as for my people, their oppressors have stripped them of their goods: the people of the land have used oppression, and committed robbery: they afflicted the needy and poor (Ezek 22:29).

Second, women, by drawing them to sensual desire and even to idolatry, as is told of Solomon in 1 Kings 11, and as to this he says: their women have ruled over them: give not the power of your soul to a woman, lest she enter upon your strength (Sir 9:2).

Third, prophets, by deceiving through the cunning of flattery, and as to this he says: O my people, as if to say: I had been accustomed to speak to you through the prophets, but because they are deceitful, I will speak to you myself, lest he not seem credible because one prophet is against another.

The same deceive you, in promising security; and destroy, in offering an occasion of sin: thus says the Lord concerning the prophets that make my people err: that bite with their teeth, and preach peace (Mic 3:5); the prophets say to them: you shall not see the sword, and there shall be no famine among you, but he will give you true peace in this place (Jer 14:13).

The Lord stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples. The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people, and with its princes. The people, which was deceived through simplicity and inexperience, is still called the people of God, and is therefore judged that it may be saved. Nor does the Lord sit in the attire of one judging, as we read in Daniel: Thrones were set, and books were opened (Dan 7:9); but he stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples, wishing those to stand whose way had been scattered. But against the princes and elders of his people he comes to judgment, not to judge but to be judged alike with them, giving them room for defense, if they can have anything to answer, according to what is said in the fiftieth psalm: That you may be justified in your words, and may overcome when you are judged (Verse 6). In the prophet Micah too we read something of the kind (Mic 6), which we have interpreted in its place. This present passage, then, is taken against the Pharisees and the Δευτερωτὰς. And between the old men and the princes there was, I think, in the old people what there is now between the elders and the bishops.

114. The Lord stands up to judge. Here the judgment for punishing the oppressors is introduced, and this is divided into two parts:

in the first, the judgment against the oppressing princes is set out,

in the second, the judgment against the women, where it says, and the Lord said (Isa 3:16).

The false prophets were deceiving the people to despoil them, and therefore they have the same judgment as the princes: they violated me among my people, for a handful of barley, and a piece of bread (Ezek 13:19).

Concerning the first, he does three things.

First, the judge is introduced; hence he says: the Lord stands up to judge: he shall judge many peoples (Mic 4:3); the judgment sat, and the books were opened (Dan 7:10).

But, says someone, "Are these things to be understood of the Lord? Could the Lord be held prisoner by men and dragged to judgment?" Of this also the same prophet shall convince you. For he says, "The Lord himself shall come into judgment with the elders and princes of the people." The Lord is judged then according to the prophet's testimony, and not only judged but scourged and slapped on the face with the palms [of men's hands], and spit on, and suffers every insult and indignity for our sake. And because all who should hear these things preached by the apostles would be perfectly amazed, therefore also the prophet speaking in their person exclaims, "Lord, who has believed our report?" For it is incredible that God, the Son of God, should be spoken of and preached as having suffered these things. For this reason they are foretold by the prophets, lest any doubt should spring up in those who are about to believe.

For you have grazed down my vineyard: the plunder of the poor is in your house. Why do you wear down my people, and grind the faces of the poor?, or crush them, and as the Seventy interpreted, put them to confusion. He keeps the prophetic custom of suddenly changing the persons: for above the Lord himself had said, My people, those who call you blessed, they deceive you; and afterwards the Prophet had added, The Lord stands to judge: the Lord will come to judgment. Therefore after the prophet, the Lord himself, who had come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes, speaks to them and rebukes the offenders: Why do you graze down my vineyard?, of which it is written: You have brought a vine out of Egypt (Ps 79 [80]:9). And in this same prophet: The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa 5:7). This vineyard the Lord in the Gospel too let out to most wicked husbandmen, who killed the son of the householder sent to them (Matt 21). The plunder of the poor, he says, is in your houses. Take the poor man either simply, as one who needs alms, or rather as the poor in spirit, of whom it is written: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And the apostle Paul: Only, he says, that we should be mindful of the poor (Gal 2:10). And what follows, Why do you wear down my people, and grind the faces of the poor?, or put them to confusion, is plainly said to the princes of the Jews. But it can also be referred to our own princes, if they wear down the common people subject to them, and publicly reprove and confound the poor when they offend, but do not dare even to say mu to the rich who sin worse. And the plunder of the poor is in their houses when they fill their treasuries and abuse the wealth of the Church for their luxuries, and either keep for themselves or distribute to their relatives the public offerings given for the support of the poor, and make the want of others into the riches of themselves and their own.

Therefore, coming with all Angels, together with Him He shall have the Saints also. For plainly saith Isaias also, “He shall come to judgment with the elders of the people.” Those “elders of the people,” then, those but now named Angels, those thousands of many men made perfect coming from the whole world, are called Heaven.

Second, the matter is introduced; hence he says: the Lord will enter into judgment with the ancients of his people, namely, with the priests, and its princes, kings and leaders: behold I will judge between cattle and cattle, between rams and he goats (Ezek 34:17).

Third, the cause is set out: and first, the accusation of the plaintiff is introduced, when he says, you have devoured: they have eaten the flesh of my people (Mic 3:3).

Second, the rebuke of the judge is set out, when he says: why do you consume my people, afflicting them, and grind the faces of the poor, weakening them by hunger? You that oppress the needy, and crush the poor (Amos 4:1). For God himself will be both plaintiff and judge.

But shouldest thou enter into a church, thou geest forth, without getting anything but countless leers, and revilings, and curses, not from the beholders only, but also from the prophet. For straightway Isaiah, that hath the fullest voice of all, as soon as he hath seen thee, will cry out, "These things saith the Lord against the princely daughters of Sion; because they walked with a lofty neck, and with winkings of the eyes, and in their walking, trailing their garments, and mincing at the same time with their feet; the Lord shall take off their bravery, and instead of a sweet smell there shall be dust, and instead of a stomacher, thou shalt gird thyself with a cord." These things for thy gorgeous array. For not to them only are these words addressed, but to every woman that doeth like them.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 89

And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion are lifted up, and have walked with outstretched neck, and went with nods of the eyes, and clapped, and walked, and stepped with their feet in measured gait. Above, both the prophet and the Lord had rebuked both the people and the princes; now the prophetic discourse turns to the women of whom he had said before, And women have ruled over them, lest they should think themselves strangers to the crime, they on account of whose luxuries and wantonness the exactors grazed down the Lord's vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in their houses, and they wore down his people and put to confusion the faces of the poor. Some think these are truly the women of the Jews; others judge that it is said metaphorically of the cities of Judea, which are called daughters of Zion: the lesser towns, that is, villages and townships. Hence in the book of Joshua too the names of the cities are set down tribe by tribe (Josh 15), and afterwards the villages and fortresses are described and are called daughters. Others, according to tropology, take the women to be souls, which, if they walk with outstretched neck and raise themselves up in pride, and pursue not manly hardness but the softness of women, are rebuked by the prophetic discourse and lose all the ornaments of the virtues, which are described under the crescents and necklaces and jewels and bracelets, the headbands and hair-ornaments and the rest of this kind. This testimony is to be turned also against the women of the Church who walk with outstretched neck and speak with nods of the eyes and clap with their hands as well as their feet, and who, to step in measured gait, do not follow nature as their guide, but hire actors as their teachers.

116. And the Lord said. Here the divine judgment against the women is set out.

And first, their fault is laid bare,

second, their punishment is foretold, where it says, the Lord will make bald (Isa 3:17).

The first of these is divided into two:

in the first, he denounces them for their pride,

in the second, for their lasciviousness, where it says, and wanton glances of their eyes.

Concerning the first, he does two things.

In the first, he denounces pride in the heart, when he says: because the daughters of Zion are haughty, in their pride: Lord, my heart is not exalted (Ps 130[131]:1).

Second, he denounces the sign of pride in the body: they have walked with stretched out necks, which is a sign of pride: he has run against him with his neck raised up, and is armed with a fat neck (Job 15:26).

117. And wanton glances. Here he denounces their lasciviousness in four things, by which they provoke men to sensual desire.

First, in sight itself; hence he says, and wanton glances: let not your heart covet her beauty, be not caught with her winks (Prov 6:25).

Second, in play: and made a noise, the Gloss adds: in playing: use not much the company of her that is a dancer . . . lest you perish by the force of her charms (Sir 9:4).

Third, in walking, as they walked: a woman talkative and wandering, not bearing to be quiet, not able to abide still at home (Prov 7:10–11).

Fourth, in lascivious adornment: in a set pace, the Gloss adds, adorned with the plunder of the poor. Behold a woman meets him in harlot's attire, prepared to deceive souls (Prov 7:10).

131. Next we consider dancing games: whether they may be practiced without sin, because of what it says in 3:16, and they made a noise as they walked with their feet and moved in a set pace: for he denounces it as sin.

To this is to be said that a game is not evil in itself; for otherwise there would not be in games the virtue which is called eutrapelia; but in as far as it is ordered to a different end, and is clothed in different circumstances, it can be an act of virtue or vice. For because it is impossible to always work in the active or contemplative life, therefore it is proper sometimes to interpose joys among our cares, lest the soul be broken by excessive severity, and so that afterwards man may more promptly be free for works of the virtues. And if the games occur for such an end and with other [proper] circumstances, it will be an act of virtue, and it can be meritorious if it is informed by grace. However, it seems that these circumstances especially are to be observed in a dancing game: that the person not be unbecoming, as a cleric or religious; that it be in a time of joyfulness, as in gratitude for liberation, or weddings and things of this kind; that it be with decent persons and with decent songs; and that the gestures not be too lascivious, and so forth. If, however, they occur for provoking lasciviousness, and according to other improper circumstances, it is certain that it will be a vicious act.

132. Next we consider the adornment of women: whether it be lawful for women to adorn themselves. And it seems that it is not, from what is said here and from 1 Timothy 2:9–10: not with plaited hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly attire: but, as it becomes women professing godliness, with good works.

And to this is to be said that adornment is to be measured to the manner and measure of the person and to the intention. For if women wear appropriate adornments according to their dignity and status so that they bear themselves with moderation in their deeds according to the custom of their native land, it will be an act of the virtue of modesty, which prescribes one's manner in walking, standing, dress, and all exterior motions; and it can be meritorious, if it be with grace; similarly, if she acts to decently please her husband (whom she already has or whom she is bound to accept), and so that he be drawn back from other women. If, however, they wear adornments that are more precious than suits them, it will be arrogance, or even something deformed by the vice of lust, if they act to provoke sensual desire for themselves.

The Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and will lay bare their hair, and instead of adornment there will be disgrace. This will befall us too whose sins are concealed, when that which is written has been fulfilled: Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed (Luke 8:17). For so long as we are covered by the hair and garment of ignorance, and men think us, who are within full of dead men's bones, to be whitened sepulchers (Matt 23), we seem to have some cleanness. But when what is hidden has been laid open, all the hair will be taken away, and a foul baldness will appear to all.

And the crescents, and the necklaces, and the jewels, and the bracelets, and the headbands, and the hair-ornaments, and the anklets, and the little chains, and the scent-boxes, and the earrings, and the rings, and the gems hanging on the forehead. He describes the jewels of the women, and through them the insignia of the cities; or, according to the anagogy, the ornaments of the various virtues. Women have little bosses hanging down in the likeness of the moon, which we transfer to the ornaments of the Church, which is illumined by the sun of righteousness. Necklaces too, hanging down as far as the breast, show the understanding and the ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) of the mind in the heart. And jewels, which in a single word signify all ornaments; and the good works of bracelets, such as Rebecca received at her betrothal (Gen 24); and headbands, the ornaments of the head; hair-ornaments, that it may have judgment of each thing; and anklets, by which our step is adorned, that we may hear: Your foot will not stumble (Ps 90 [91]); and: He will rescue my feet from falling (Ps 55 [56]); and little chains, which are woven of rods of gold and silver, that is, of the sense and the words of the Scriptures; and scent-boxes, that we may be the good odor of Christ (2 Cor 2:15); and earrings, that we may not hear the judgment of blood, but the words of the Lord who says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Luke 8:8); and rings, with which we are sealed for the service of the Lord, whom God the Father has sealed. Hence it is said to the prince of Tyre: You are the seal of likeness (Ezek 28:12). The prodigal son too received a ring with the robe (Luke 15), and shoes; and gems hanging on the forehead, by which our faces are adorned. Of the adornment of this head we read in the psalm as well: Like ointment on the head, which runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron (Ps 132 [133]:1). Although the Seventy Translators, Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translate all these in different ways, we have woven them together as we could, either from the Hebrew or from their translation; nor do we wish to linger longer on each, lest the exposition become trifling and produce weariness in the prudent reader.

In that day the Lord will take away the adornment of the shoes. In what day? The Jews think, that of the Babylonian captivity. We prove that it is more truly when they were taken by the Romans and lost all the ornaments of clothing and gems, of gold and jewels, and their various furnishings. Or else, through the metaphor of the women, all the adornment of the cities is related to have been destroyed. Understand the ornaments of the cities to be in the streets and porticoes, the forum and the gymnasia and the public walls. If we refer these to the state of souls, let us recall that we have read of the shod feet of him who is to eat the flesh of the lamb and celebrate the Pasch, and that neither the garments nor the shoes of those passing through the wilderness were worn out. What are these shoes? Those of which the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: Your feet shod in preparation of the Gospel of peace (Eph 6:15). These shoes souls will lose when they walk with outstretched neck and drag their garments with their feet, and instead of matronly cleanness sweep up the filth of the ground.

119. In that day. Here he takes away artificial adornments from them:

and first, things which pertain to the adornment of their members,

second, things which pertain to the care of adornments, where it says, crisping pins, and looking-glasses (Isa 3:22).

Concerning the first, he does two things:

first, he takes away things which pertain to the adornment of parts;

second, things which pertain to the adornment of the whole, where it says, and changes of apparel (Isa 3:22).

Concerning the first, he does two things:

first, he takes away things which pertain to the members of the body;

second, things which pertain especially to the sense organs, where it says, sweet balls (Isa 3:20).

Concerning the first, he does two things:

first, he takes away things which pertain to the lower parts of the body;

second, things which pertain especially to the parts of the head, where it says, and headbands (Isa 3:23).

120. Therefore, he first says, as to the feet, the ornaments of shoes, of any kind, and especially, little moons, that is, certain pictures on shoes made from gilded leather: how beautiful are your feet in shoes, O prince's daughter (Song 7:1).

Second, as to the neck: chains, certain adornments of the neck, which hang down to the breast and are given in honor of a victory: that grace may be added to your head, and a chain of gold to your neck (Prov 1:9).

Third, as to the breast, he says, necklaces, any adornments, but especially buckles by which the breast is secured, lest a garment be opened: the joints of your thighs are like necklaces, that are made by the hand of a skillful workman. (Song 7:1).

Fourth, as to the arms, he says, bracelets, adornments of the arms, named from armus ("shoulder," usually of an animal): both men and women gave bracelets . . . to make the work of the tabernacle of the testimony (Exod 32:21–22).

121. And bonnets. Here he places adornments of the head;

and first, those for the top of the head: bonnets, adornments of the head like a crown: she put a bonnet upon her head (Jdt 10:3).

Second, as to the hair, he says, bodkins, certain instruments of silver or gold made like sharpened sticks, by which women divide the hair before their brows, as is said of Judith in the same place: she plaited the hair of her head (Jdt 10:3).

122. Third, as to the neck, he touches on two things.

First, ornaments of the legs, from peri, which means "around," and colon, which means "member," as if to say, "adorned around a member." Haymo says that it is made from gold, similar to bracelets, and it is placed around the neck. The Gloss says that it is worn above the foot, like a bracelet; others says that they are certain adornments placed around the borders of garments like golden fringe, or some hides, or something of this kind. And this can stand with either of these meanings, because thus they are both around the neck and around the feet; for garments have such adornments both on the hood and on the lower edges, and thus they adorn the neck mediately: therefore we offer as gifts to the Lord what gold every one of us could find in the booty, in ornaments of the legs and bracelets, rings (Num 31:50).

123. Second, he places immediate adornments of the neck, when he says, tablets, namely, certain chains, with gold and silver rods like the larvae of a moray eel, which are placed around the neck: we will make you tablets of gold, with larvae of silver (Song 1:10). And because the neck is between the head and the body, its adornment redounds to both, and therefore it may be placed with either.

124. And sweet balls. Here is placed things which pertain to the sense organs,

and first, as to smell: sweet balls, certain small boxes in which they placed musk and things of this kind; or also certain vessels, like an apple made from silver, perforated like a thurible, in which is placed fire and something odiferous: we will run after you to the odor of your ointments (Song 1:3).

Second, as to hearing, earrings, that is, certain rings of gold or silver, placed in the ears of women, which have been pierced for this purpose: she decked herself out with her earrings, and with her jewels, and went after her lovers (Hos 2:13).

Third, as to touch, which is strongest in the fingers: rings: therefore we offer . . . rings (Num 31:50).

Fourth, as to sight: jewels hanging on the forehead, with which the women of Egypt were adorned: you shall take onyx stones, and precious stones to adorn the ephod and the rational (Exod 25:7). He makes no mention of taste, because its instrument is interior and is not adorned.

And the pins, and the mirrors, and the fine linens, and the fillets, and the summer veils. Women have pins, by which the arrangement of the dressed hair is held together, so that it may not flow too loosely and be scattered into straggling locks. They have mirrors too, in which they look at their face, and if they see anything lacking, they add to their adornment. They have fine linens, which are called wraps; and fillets, with which the hair is bound, which they call ταινίας. They have summer veils too, which we can call mantles, with which Rebecca also was covered; and today too the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia are veiled with them. In Hebrew they are called ARDIDIM, in Greek θέριστρα, from the fact that in θέρει, that is, in summer and the heat, they protect the bodies of women. The daughters of Zion, therefore, because of their pride lost the pins by which the rule of all the precepts was held fast. They lost the mirrors which the women staying at the doors of the tabernacle offered in Exodus for making the laver of the Lord (Exod 38); of which the apostle Paul too spoke: But now we see through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor 13:12). They lost the fine linens and the fillets, with which they covered their shoulders and bound fast the mind that flowed this way and that; and the summer veils, with which they were covered as by a most safe shade in the heats. We say these things lest we seem altogether to shun the tropology of this place. But it is a very great labor to linger on each item and to seek a broad explanation.

And the changes of raiment, and the mantles, and the linen cloths. For linen cloths the Seventy interpreted transparent Laconian garments, wishing to signify the very fine garments with which the bodies of the Lacedaemonians were covered, who were most ready for war and of a rather austere life; although neither the Hebrew nor any other of the translators has Laconian. Changes of raiment and mantles, which Symmachus translated more expressively ἀναβολαια, are ornaments of women's clothing, by which the shoulders and breasts are covered. Changes of raiment, according to the anagogy, are those of which it is said: They will go from strength to strength (Ps 83 [84]:8); and linen cloths, that, washed in the Lord, we may enjoy delights, according to what is written in the Psalms: You will give them to drink of the torrent of your pleasure (Ps 35 [36]:9). But all these things the daughters of Zion lost, because they walked with outstretched neck and with nods of the eyes made a show of pride, thinking that what they had was of their own power and not of the grace of the Lord.

125. And changes of apparel. Here he places adornments pertaining to the whole body,

and first, those for clothing the body, and thus he says, changes of apparel, that is, various pairs of garments: have clothed you with change of garments. And he said: put a miter (Zech 3:4–5).

Second, those for covering the body, and thus he says, cloaks: but she quickly took her cloak, and covered herself (Gen 24:65).

Third, those for lying in, and thus he says, fine linen: then comes Peter . . . and went into the sepulcher: and saw the linen cloths lying (John 20:6).

126. And crisping pins. Here he places things which pertain to the care of adornments.

And first, things for arranging them: crisping pins: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven (Matt 19:24).

Second, things for discerning them, and looking-glasses, by which women discern whether they are well adorned: he made also the laver of brass, with the foot thereof, of the looking-glasses of the women that watched at the door of the tabernacle (Exod 38:8).

Third, things for covering adornments;

and first, things for covering adornments of the shoulders: and lawns, fine-spun veils with which the shoulders are covered, as are made by women in Campania: she made fine linen, and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Chanaanite (Prov 31:24).

Second, for covering the adornments of the head: headbands, that is, pepla; or better, what are called ligamenta, with which women bind their hair, made like a net; and thus may be taken Exodus 28:37: and you shall tie it with a violet headband, namely, a plate of purest gold (Exod 28:36), where was written the holy name of the Lord.

Third, for covering the adornments of the whole body, he says, fine veils. The Gloss says, the most fine of feminine garments, pervious to sight, suitable for summer, from which it gets its name, for "theria" means "summer". And women were especially accustomed to carry such things over silk garments: she put off the garments of her widowhood, and took a veil (Gen 38:14). About many of these, it is said in Ezekiel 16:10–12: I clothed you with embroidery, and shod you with violet colored shoes: and I girded you about with fine linen, and clothed you with fine garments . . . and put bracelets on your hands, and a chain about your neck, and I put a jewel upon your forehead and earrings in your ears, and a beautiful crown upon your head.

And instead of a sweet odor there will be a stench, and instead of a girdle, a cord. The penitent says that sins stink: My wounds have putrefied and are corrupted because of my folly (Ps 37 [38]:6). The Apostle commanded the loins to be girded with a girdle, saying: Stand, having your loins girded in truth (Eph 6:14). And of the sinner we read: Each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22). Therefore, instead of the good odor of the virtues, the daughters of Zion will have the rottenness of sins; and instead of the girdle of truth they will be bound with the cords of falsehood, such as those had upon their heads who with rags and filth begged their life from the king of Syria.

And instead of a breast-band, haircloth. For breast-band, as Symmachus interpreted it, the Seventy translated a tunic μεσοπορφύραν, that is, striped with purple, which Aquila expressed as girdle of exultation. Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, PHTHIGIL (פתיגיל), which is a kind of women's ornament. The band covers the breast, and holds that place in women which the Rational holds in the High Priests. Of this breast-band Jeremiah too spoke in mystical speech: If a bride can forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band, I too will forget you, says the Lord (Jer 2:32). The virgin, such as the Apostle desires to present us to Christ (2 Cor 11), so long as she is not corrupted in Egypt and her breasts, which are bound with the breast-band, are not broken, is joined to the bridegroom; and though daily she bears sons of the virtues, she by no means ceases to be a virgin. But if at some time she has spread her feet to every passer-by and followed her lovers, and, according to the prophecy of Hosea, the Lord has hedged in her ways and shut off her paths, she will return to her former husband and will hear: Put off the garments of mourning, and put on the garments of your glory (Hos 2).

127. And instead of a sweet smell there shall be. Here, the adornments of lasciviousness having been taken away, he exchanges them for the care of misery.

And first, as to that which is without, he says: instead of a sweet smell there shall be stench: for smell comes from without: his stench shall ascend, and his rottenness shall go up, because he has done proudly (Joel 2:20).

Second, as to that which is around, he says, instead of a girdle, a cord: he looses the belt of kings, and girds their loins with a cord (Job 12:18).

Third, as to that which is above, he says, instead of curled hair, baldness.

Fourth, as to that which is within: instead of a stomacher, according to the Gloss, with which the breasts are bound together, that is, squeezed together, lest from their size they convey shamefulness.

Your most beautiful men too shall fall by the sword, and your strong ones in battle. For most beautiful men the Seventy interpreted, and your most beautiful son, whom you love, shall fall by the sword. If we understand this of the state of a soul which has sinned after the virtues, let us take her most beautiful son to be good works, which have fallen by the enemy's sword; and the strong too to have perished in battle, because the righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in whatever day he has gone astray (Ezek 33:12). But if we follow the history, we shall be taught by these words that the prophet's discourse is not about women whose husbands fell in battle, but about the cities of Judea, which he called daughters of Zion, and whose warriors fell in the conflict. Lastly, the following verse speaks of the same Zion.

128. Your fairest men. Here he takes away the comfort of men from them as to four things.

Women delight in the beauty of men, and as to this, he says: your fairest men also shall fall by the sword: her Nazarites were whiter than snow, purer than milk, more ruddy than the old ivory, fairer than the sapphire (Lam 4:7).

Second, in their fortitude, and as to this, he says, and your valiant ones, below: they have led away the strong ones thereof into captivity (Isa 23:13).

And her gates shall lament and mourn, and the city itself, desolate, shall sit upon the ground. This we see with our eyes to this day. According to tropology the interpretation is easy: that whoever has given place to the devil and has not kept his heart with all watchfulness, his gates mourn; and, the bridegroom being absent, he is ever in mourning, and, falling from the heights, sits in the dust of the earth.

Third, delight in their dignity, and as to this, he says: her gates, that is, the judges sitting in the gates, shall lament, inwardly, and mourn, outwardly: her gates are destroyed in the ground: he has destroyed, and broken her bars, her king (Lam 2:9).

Fourth, they delight in the joyfulness of men, and as to this, he says: and she shall sit desolate on the ground: he has made me desolate, wasted with sorrow all the day long (Lam 1:13).
4:
The "seven women" suffer "reproach" and go about seeking to receive the one who is able to "take away their reproach". These same "seven women" make a promise, that they will "eat their own bread and be clothed with their own garments". They have no need of the "bread" of him who "takes away their reproach"; they do not lack the "garments of a man" whom they "take". They have better "garments" than a "man" can supply to them; they have more sumptuous foods than the human condition can bestow. It is therefore worth considering whose these "seven women" are and what their "reproach" is. The "seven women" are one; for they are the "Spirit of God". And this one is seven; for the "Spirit of God" is "the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord". This "wisdom" suffers "reproach" from the many wisdoms that rise up against it; this true "understanding" bears "reproach" from false understandings; this great "counsel" is reproached by many counsels that are not good; this "might" is reviled by a certain thing which, though it is not "might", promises that it is "might"; this "knowledge" suffers "reproach" from a certain "knowledge" of false name that filches its name; this "piety" is reproached by that which, though it calls itself "piety", is impiety and instructs the impious; this "fear" suffers "reproach" from that which is thought to be "fear"; for many promise a divine dread, but they do not fear "with knowledge". Let us therefore consider in what way these "seven" suffer "reproach". See the "wisdom of this world", see the "wisdom of the princes of this world", how they reproach the "wisdom" of my Christ, how they reproach the "wisdom" of the true Judaism, according to which we are circumcised spiritually, while those others are cut off. Understand, then, how the "wisdom of this world and of the princes of this world" reviles "wisdom"; and on this account a "man" is sought who may be with these "seven" spiritual "women", that he may "take away their reproach". Properly there is "one" "man" who may "take away their reproach". Who is this "man"? Jesus, who "came forth according to the flesh" "from the root of Jesse", "made of the seed of David according to the flesh, predestined the Son of God in power according to the spirit of justification". For "there came forth a rod from the root of Jesse". The "rod" is not "the firstborn of all creation", the "rod" is not "he who in the beginning was with God, God the Word", but "a rod from the root of Jesse", who "was born according to the flesh". "There came forth", therefore, "a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root". What is the "flower" and what is the "root"? For both are one in him who lies beneath; but the difference is one of dealings. For if you are a sinner, there is no "flower" for you, nor will you see the "flower which is from the root of Jesse"; for the "rod" will come even to you, just as the disciple speaks of the "rod" and the "flower". Of the "rod" indeed he says: "what do you wish? shall I come to you with a rod?", but of the "flower": "or in the love of God and the spirit of gentleness?". "There came forth", therefore, "from the root of Jesse a rod" for him who is punished with penalties, a "rod" for him who needs rebuke, a "rod" for him who has need to be reproved; but a "flower" for him who is already instructed and does not need harsh correction, or at least does not need punishments, but is now strong enough to begin to flower toward perfect fruit. For first the "flower" is shown, and then after the "flower" it becomes a "rod" unto fruit. "There came forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root. And the seven women shall rest, the Spirit of God, the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him". For the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in Moses, the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in Joshua son of Nun, the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in each of the prophets, in Isaiah, in Jeremiah.

But do not stone me as though I were blaspheming, while I desire to glorify my Lord Jesus Christ; rather, bearing with me, consider what is said, and you will see that in none of them did the "spirit rest", not because it came to none, but because it "rested" in none. It came "upon" Moses, and Moses does not believe after the "spirit of wisdom" that came to him. For he says: "Hear, you rebels: shall I bring forth water for you out of this rock?" It came "upon" all the just, it came also "upon" Isaiah. But what does he say? "Having unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips". The "spirit of wisdom" came after that "tongs" and fire, it came to him "having unclean lips", but it did "not rest". It used him indeed as a minister, but it did "not rest"; it is troubled, to whatever of men it comes. For every man sins, "there is no just man upon the earth who does good and does not sin"; "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day, but his months are numbered". Therefore it "rests upon" none. We can also prove from the Gospel that the "spirit came upon" many and "did not remain in" them. A little while ago it was read: "my spirit shall not remain in these men forever"; he does not say: it shall not be, but: "it shall not remain". John saw one alone in whom it "remained", and this was the sign: "upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the Son of God". A certain one ministered to the Word of God when the "spirit descended"; a little after he "sins", a little after he speaks an "idle word". But I do not know whether he even remains without sin; do you think that, with the "spirit" present, it is granted to sin? "Upon" none, therefore, did "the Spirit of God rest", according to what is written: "there came forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of understanding, the spirit of counsel and might". On account of this he is the "angel of great counsel", on account of this he grew strong and, growing strong, ascended, and the powers marvel at him as he ascends and say of him: this is "the Lord strong and mighty in battle". To him, then, as he ascends into the heavenly places, or to his strength, I will say that: "the spirit of counsel and might rested upon him"; "the Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become for me salvation". "There rested", therefore, "upon him the Spirit of God, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of God filled him".

The "women", therefore, seeking whom they may "take, seven shall lay hold of one man". And this depends on what precedes, and one must first know when the "seven women receive one man". When the "strong ones" of Jerusalem "have been humbled", when the "cases of the ornament" of the daughters of Zion "have mourned", when she "has been left" "alone", when she "has been dashed to the ground", then "seven women shall lay hold of one man, saying: we will eat our own bread, and we will be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be invoked upon us", then "did they lay hold" and truly hold fast "seven women, one man", Jesus Christ our Lord, according to which he is understood to be "man", according to which he was born, according to which he took up a body. "Seven women shall lay hold of one man, saying: we will eat our own bread". Many "men" walk about and the "women lay hold" of none, no "man" pleases them; for it is not on account of a scarcity of men that they "lay hold of one man", but on account of the rarity of the "man" such as they wished, such as they sought; "one" "man" only they found, whom they "laid hold of", that they might "say" to him: "we will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments". There is a certain food of "wisdom", there is likewise a certain food both of "understanding" and of the other "spirits". What is this food? I am not afraid to say: there is another food beyond these; perhaps, as my food is the word of God, who says: "I am the living bread who came down from heaven" and "I give life to the world", so the food of "wisdom" is the Father himself, on account of this: "my food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to complete his work". Nor is it to be thought that "wisdom" and "understanding" and the rest of the "spirits" lack anything, because they have another food, since of the whole dispensation there is one food, the nature of God. "We will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments". There is a certain adornment of "wisdom", with which it is adorned; "wisdom" is adorned with speech. Each of these "women" has her adornments. "Only let your name be invoked upon us, take away our reproach". What is the "name of wisdom"? Jesus. What is: "let your name be invoked upon us"? I am "wisdom", I wish to be called by your name, that I, "wisdom", may be called Jesus, that "understanding" and "great counsel" and "might" and "knowledge" and "piety" and "the fear of God" may be named Jesus, that your "name" may become "all in all". "Let your name be invoked upon us, take away our reproach". Truly Jesus "took away the reproach". Therefore, rising up, let us pray to God, who sent this "man" and in whom "the spirit of the seven women rested", that this "man" may grant to us also the fellowship of these "women", and that, taking them up, we may become wise and understanding in God, and that the other virtues may adorn our soul in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages, Amen!".

"And He had in His right hand seven stars." He said that in His right hand He had seven stars, because the Holy Spirit of sevenfold agency was given into His power by the Father. As Peter exclaimed to the Jews: "Being at the right hand of God exalted, He hath shed forth this Spirit received from the Father, which ye both see and hear." Moreover, John the Baptist had also anticipated this, by saying to his disciples: "For God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto Him. The Father," says he, "loveth the Son, and hath given all things into His hands." Those seven stars are the seven churches, which he names in his addresses by name, old calls them to whom he wrote epistles. Not that they are themselves the only, or even the principal churches; but what he says to one, he says to all. For they are in no respect different, that on that ground any one should prefer them to the larger number of similar small ones. In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: "That thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the Church of the living God." We read also that this typical number is announced by the Holy Spirit by the month of Isaiah: "Of seven women which took hold of one man." The one man is Christ, not born of seed; but the seven women are seven churches, receiving His bread, and clothed with his apparel, who ask that their reproach should be taken away, only that His name should be called upon them. The bread is the Holy Spirit, which nourishes to eternal life, promised to them, that is, by faith. And His garments wherewith they desire to be clothed are the glory of immortality, of which Paul the apostle says: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on mortality." Moreover, they ask that their reproach may be taken away-that is, that they may be cleansed from their sins: for the reproach is the original sin which is taken away in baptism, and they begin to be called Christian men, which is, "Let thy name be called upon us." Therefore in these seven churches, of one Catholic Church are believers, because it is one in seven by the quality of faith and election. Whether writing to them who labour in the world, and live of the frugality of their labours, and are patient, and when they see certain men in the Church wasters, and pernicious, they hear them, lest there should become dissension, he yet admonishes them by love, that in what respects their faith is deficient they should repent; or to those who dwell in cruel places among persecutors, that they should continue faithful; or to those who, under the pretext of mercy, do unlawful sins in the Church, and make them manifest to be done by others; or to those that are at ease in the Church; or to those who are negligent, and Christians only in name; or to those who are meekly instructed, that they may bravely persevere in faith; or to those who study the Scriptures, and labour to know the mysteries of their announcement, and are unwilling to do God's work that is mercy and love: to all he urges penitence, to all he declares judgment.
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

HOW DO THE SEVEN WOMEN MENTIONED IN ISAIAH, “AND SEVEN WOMEN SHALL TAKE HOLD,” ETC. (Isa. 4:1), SIGNIFY THE SEVEN CATHOLIC CHURCHES? — “And seven women,” he says, “shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach.” It is absolutely clear that by the seven women the seven Churches are signified: for although the Church is one, it is called sevenfold, so that the one body may consist of a sevenfold number of members. For not only we, but also the citizens above are members of the Church, whose head is Christ (Eph. 5:23). Whether therefore the Churches are called one or seven does not conflict. It is called one because it has one head, which is Christ; it is called seven because, just as the members are diverse, so also the spiritual powers, among which we too are reckoned, have diverse functions, on account of which they are called “of the air.” They are diverse for this reason, that not each one can do all things, but all together are the body of Christ: for he is the head of the body, the Church (Col. 1:18), from whom the whole body exists, that is, from whom all things in heaven and on earth have their origin. In this Church which is on earth, mention is made of all the Churches: for when in it the mystery of the Creator is proclaimed, this teaching is also revealed to the heavenly beings. When it is made known to those below, it is necessary that those above also hear. Therefore the Apostle says, “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God who created all things, so that through the Church the diverse wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3:8). Through this Church, therefore, the heavenly beings are taught, because “Truth,” it says, “has sprung out of the earth” (Ps. 85:12). In order that mention of the higher ones might be made, seven Churches are here named in one people, and these seven Churches the prophet presents as suppliants to the Savior made man. For they understood that Christ was born for this purpose, that he might take away reproof, first indeed of those who were living under his Law, and then of the rest. They had also in memory that it was written, “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn ungodliness away from Jacob” (Isa. 59:20). These seven Churches therefore laid hold of one man, that is, of Christ born, saying, “We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach.” (Isa. 4:1) What is it that they pray for? If they use their own bread and are clothed with their own garments, that is, if they live and are not naked, what do they lack? For if bread signifies life, and clothing signifies being clothed with God, for whoever is without God is called naked, therefore the Apostle says, “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27); and again, “So that we may not be found naked when unclothed” (2 Cor. 5:3): what is it that they ask, that their reproach may be taken away, unless that this people is signified in the number of the seven Churches, which, living under the Law, was expecting Christ promised for the abolition of sins? Therefore they say, “We will eat our own bread,” that is, we will be fed by the words of the Law which hand on the one God: for “Not by bread alone does man live, but by every word of God” (Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4). “And we will wear our own apparel,” that is, we will be known by the name of our Creator: for each person is said to be clothed in that which he is and professes. Indeed, senators or officials are understood from their garments to be what they are. But because these things are not sufficient to win God’s favor, it was further ordained that through the mystery of the knowledge of the one God, man should become heir of the kingdom of heaven. For cleansed from sins by faith, and alienated from the second death (which, by the judgment pronounced on Adam, kept men in the underworld), held by none, he goes into the paradise of God the Father, of which the Lord said to the thief that he would be with him there (Luke 23:43). For although the aforesaid people, signified by the seven Churches, was under God’s law, and by devotion bound both for its own sin and for its ancestral sin, “For all,” he says, “have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23)—therefore the Churches mentioned above pray that their reproach may be taken away by the call of the name of Christ: for those who bear his sign, by which he conquered death, cannot be held by the enemy. And not only these Churches pray that the name of Christ be called upon them, but also the spiritual ones above, dwelling in the heavens. For although the spiritual and heavenly powers are such, yet they are subject to reproach if they are alienated from their Creator, and they will not be members of the body if, not recognizing their head, they wander. And the prophet bears witness in the following words to what we have explained, saying, “In that day God shall give light by counsel upon the earth.” And he added, “For the Lord shall wash away,” he says, “the filth of the sons and daughters, and shall purge the blood from their midst” (Isaiah 4:2, according to the LXX). What is more evident than that in that day, that is, when the promise of God was fulfilled and the mystery of faith was declared to men, they were enlightened, so that, purified through knowledge of the Creator, those who had been guilty of death might become heirs of eternal life? The prophet therefore spoke in a general way, so as to signify that all need the gift of God, so that both sinners and righteous may be known to have awaited the mercy of God: sinners on account of their own offenses, that they might be snatched from the jaws of death; and the righteous, absolved from their ancestral sin, with the sentence given in Adam wiped out, by which all were held by death, might enter the kingdom of God with the liberty received, now made not servants, but sons of God.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 47: HOW THE SEVEN WOMEN OF ISAIAH SIGNIFY THE SEVEN CHURCHES

And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying: We will eat our own bread, and be covered with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us: take away our reproach. When the most beautiful men of the city of Jerusalem have fallen by the sword, and the strong have perished in battle, and her gates have lamented and mourned, and she herself has been made desolate through the very great scarcity of men, the warriors having been slain, seven women will take hold of one man, desiring to have seed in Zion and a household in Jerusalem, saying that they have food and clothing, only so that they may not be seen to be without a husband and lie under that curse which is written: Cursed is the barren woman, and she who does not make seed in Israel (Deut 7). Zechariah too agrees with this sense: In those days ten men out of all the tongues of the nations shall take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you (Zech 8:23). The numbers seven and ten are familiar to the Jews on account of the sabbath and the ten precepts of the Law, and therefore they make frequent use of them; although, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, in which they interpret the word SABA (שבע) now as seven, now as many, now as oath, it may in this place signify not seven but many. This is according to the letter. But at the coming of the Lord and Savior, seven women, that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, of which the same Prophet is going to speak in what follows: There shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root; and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him (Isa 11:1, 2), will take hold of Jesus, whom they had long desired, because they had been able to find no other in whom they might rest in an everlasting abode. Hence John the Baptist too relates in the Gospel: And he who sent me said to me himself: He upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he it is (John 1:33). In Zechariah too we read of seven eyes upon one stone, and on one golden lampstand seven lamps and seven pipes, and two olive trees on either side of the lamp, founded with a firm root (Zech 3). And that the grace of the Holy Spirit possesses all things needs no exposition. But because among men it always suffered reproach, no one living as the gifts of the Holy Spirit demanded, therefore they desire the name of Jesus to be called upon them, so that what was imperfect in the Law may be completed in the Gospel.

And in Isaiah we read: Seven women shall take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us, take away our reproach. Those, then, who there are called seven women, that is, Churches, whose number is contained also in the apostle Paul — for he writes to seven churches, to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, to the Thessalonians. And in the Apocalypse of John the Lord, girded with variety and with purest gold, walks in the midst of the seven lampstands, that is, of the churches of the Ephesians, the Smyrnaeans, the Pergamenes, the Thyatirans, the Sardians, the Philadelphians, the Laodiceans —, are now named ten in the prophet Zechariah, whom the Lord also sought, so that, if he had found them in Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, he might deliver them from destruction.

Second, their fecundity is represented by the seven women in Isaiah: Seven women will take hold of one man on that day. A man, because these virtues produce virility; and one, because they do not divide him, but make him stable and fruitful.

133. And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man. After he denounces the calumny of the oppressors in chapters 2 and 3, in this chapter, the prophet sets out the consolation of the oppressed. And this is divided into two parts:

in the first, he consoles them against the oppression of women;

in the second, against the oppression of tyrants, where it says, in that day (Isa 4:2).

134. Now women are accustomed to be troublesome to men in three matters, namely, in contempt of men, and as to this, he says: and in that day seven women shall take hold: which the Gloss explains literally, that it could have been that after the captivity, many men having been killed, there remained more women than men, so that seven women sought to have one man, below: a man shall be more precious than gold, yea a man than the finest of gold (Isa 13:12).

Second, they were accustomed to be troublesome in superfluous food and clothing, and as to this he says: we will eat our own bread, as if to say: it will not be necessary that he give expenses to them: she is like the merchant's ship, she brings her bread from afar. She has sought wool and flax, and has wrought by the counsel of her hands (Prov 31:13–14).

Third, they are troublesome in the haughtiness of pride, and as to this he says: only let your name be called upon us, that we may be called your wives, take away our reproach, namely, of barrenness. No one shall be barren among you of either sex, neither of men nor cattle (Deut 7:14).

135. But from this it seems that it may be lawful to have many wives, because the Lord never consoles through something unlawful. Moreover, every sin is unnatural; but for one man to have many wives is natural, because one man can impregnate many women.

To this is to be said that, as the Philosopher says, the joining of male and female among men is not only for the sake of generation, as in brute animals, but also for advantage of life: hence male and female have different operations, by which they give help to each other. Therefore, as far as something is otherwise ordered to these ends, so far is it otherwise called natural or unnatural. For that which in no manner can stand with the stated end is entirely unnatural, and never can be good, as the vice of sodomy, and as when one woman has many husbands, since one woman cannot be impregnated by many men, and as regards civil life, because one woman is not ruled by many men, but the contrary. However, something can, considered in itself, stand indifferently in relation to the stated end; and this can be determined in various times in various ways according to various cases by a lawgiver: and it will be the positive just, as with the degrees of consanguinity.

136. There is, however, something through which someone can pursue the end, but which nevertheless impedes the end in the majority of cases. And this is, of itself, unnatural, but it can be lawful according to the dispensation of a lawgiver attending to special cases. And such is it for one man may have wives: for one man can rule many women according to civil life, and one man can impregnate many women; but, nevertheless, something presents an impediment to generation, since it is necessary for the seed of a man to be prepared, and this cannot happen with those engaging frequently in intercourse, because of which such men are frequently sterile. And yet more does it impede common life, because the perfect friendship of the sort which exists between a man and his wife, for whom man even leaves his father and mother (Gen 2:24), cannot be had with many wives.

142. The Gloss, however, touches on a twofold mystery. Some explain the seven women (Isa 4:1) as churches, and according to this, this chapter is divided into three parts:

first is placed the espousal;

second, the exaltation of the bridegroom, where it says, in that day (Isa 4:2);

third, the government of the bridegroom, where it says, and it shall come to pass (Isa 4:3).

Now the espousal is through faith: I will espouse you to me in faith (Hos 2:20). Hence he puts forth three things.

First, the communication of faith, seven women (Isa 4:1), the seven churches, of which Revelation 1:4 says: John to the seven churches which are in Asia, in which are contained all churches according to the fifth rule of Tyconius, shall take hold, through faith; one man, that is, Christ: I will take hold of you, and bring you into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that bore me (Song 8:2).

Second, the manifestation of hope, which is from receiving the sacrament: we will eat our own bread, the body of Christ given to us: the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world (John 6:52); and which is from receiving the gift of virtue: we will wear our own apparel, that is, the virtues: I clothed you with embroidery, and shod you with violet colored shoes: . . . and clothed you with fine garments, and I decked you also with ornaments (Ezek 16:10–11).
