But if anyone should say that the Hebrew books were afterward falsified by the Jews, let him hear what Origen answers to this little question in the eighth volume of his Explanations of Isaiah: that the Lord and the Apostles, who rebuke the other crimes in the Scribes and Pharisees, would never have kept silent about this crime, which was the greatest. But if they should say that the Hebrew books were falsified after the coming of the Lord and Savior and the preaching of the Apostles, I shall not be able to hold back my laughter, that the Savior and the Evangelists and the Apostles should have brought forward testimonies in such a way as the Jews were afterward going to falsify them. But of the present place this must be said: that we take refuge in the translation of the Seventy in vain, lest what is said according to the Hebrew should seem blasphemous: Hear with hearing, and do not understand: and see the vision, and do not know, since we find testimonies of this kind in the Seventy Translators too, such as that in Exodus which is said to Pharaoh: For this reason I have raised you up, to show my power in you (Exod 9:16). But if he himself raised him up and hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he should not believe; and of others it is said: God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear (Rom 11:8); and in the Psalms: Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense: let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bend their backs always (Ps 68 [69]:23-24): then those who do not see are not at fault, but he who gave them eyes for not seeing. So even apart from this testimony which we are now trying to expound, the same question remains in the Churches, and either the others will be resolved along with this one, or this one too will be insoluble along with the others. The blessed apostle Paul explains this place more fully to the Romans, and we should be doing something superfluous if we wished to comprise in a brief discourse what he pursued through almost the whole epistle. For he says, after many things: God has shut up all things in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all (Rom 11:32). And marveling at the mysteries of the Lord he added: O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways. And again, disputing about the unbelief of the Jews, he says: Have they so sinned that they should fall? God forbid; but by their offense salvation came to the Gentiles, to provoke them to emulation (Rom 11:11). And a little after: For if their casting away is the reconciliation of the world, what will their taking up be? Is it not life from the dead? And again: For I would not have you ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in yourselves, that blindness has come in part upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and then all Israel should be saved. And a little after (Rom 11:25): As concerning the Gospel they are enemies for your sakes, but as concerning the election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers: for the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance. For as you, he says, once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief: so these too have now not believed in your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. For God has shut up all things under sin, that he may have mercy on all. It is therefore not the cruelty of God but his mercy that one nation should perish so that all may be saved; that a part of the Jews should not see, so that the whole world may behold. Hence the Lord himself too in the Gospel turns the mystery of the man blind from birth, who had received his eyes, to Tropology, and says: For judgment I came into this world, that those who see may not see, and those who do not see may see (John 9:39). And in another place Simeon speaks: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising again of many (Luke 2:34). So while they do not see, we see; while they fall, we rise again. Understanding this, the Prophet in a certain manner says in other words: O Lord, you command me to speak to the people of the Jews, that they may hear and not understand the Savior, and see him and not recognize him. If you will that your command be fulfilled and the whole world be saved, which I too desire to come about, then blind the heart of this people and make its ears heavy and shut its eyes, that they may not understand, may not hear, may not see. For if they see, and are converted, and understand, and are healed, the whole world will not receive healing. From this we perceive that, however grave the sin, if anyone is converted he can be healed. And at the same time this too is to be understood: that for the greatness of their crime they were judged unworthy even of repentance, as the Lord himself says to Jerusalem: How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not (Matt 23:37).

But he appeared not so much for the eyes of human beings as for their salvation, for even though he was first seen by fleshly eyes when he was born of the virgin, still he did not appear because the eye of faith did not as yet recognize his power. Hence it is said to the Jews by the prophet: "Seeing you will see and will not see"; that is, the Savior whom they discerned with their fleshly eyes they did not see in a spiritual light.

226. Third, the office is enjoined on him; as to the double act he foretells to discuss: and he said: go: behold I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves (Matt 10:16); and you shall say to this people: and you will separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth (Jer 15:19).

227. Hearing, hear. Here the sentence is set out.

And first, the sentence of hardness of heart is set out; he does not, however, harden hearts by sending malice into them, but by not imparting grace, and this is because they do not wish to be converted to grace.

Second, the length of the sentence is sought, where it says, and I said: how long, O Lord? (Isa 6:11).

Concerning the first, he does three things.

First, the pronouncement of the sentence by the Lord is set out, as to the two senses that produce knowledge: namely hearing, which serves instruction; hence he says hear, with the outer ears, hearing, Christ, or another who preaches, and understand not, as if to say: because you do not wish it, you do not understand. This is permissive. And as to sight, which serves discovery: and see the vision, Christ, corporeally, or the mighty works of God; and know it not; this is permissive and not imperative, below: who is blind, but my servant? (Isa 42:19).

But what is the cause that the one hearing "does not understand and the one seeing does not see"? "The heart of this people", he says, "has been thickened". Since indeed this too must be understood, whence it comes, bodily and spiritual fatness are not the same, nor are bodily and spiritual thinness the same. For that which is bodily thick comes to be in the flesh, and a "fleshly heart" does me no harm if "it be thickened", nor does it profit if by illness or by whatever cause it be made thin. And I suppose that the fleshly "heart" of those who are held by fear becomes such. For as they waste away entirely from sickness, so they say that the thickness too, and whatever is fat about their "heart", is thinned out. What harm, then, does it do me if my bodily "heart" "be thickened"? And suppose too my "heart" be made thin — what profit do I have from that? But by a shared term with the bodily "heart", the ruling part of our soul is named, as is manifest from what is said in the Gospel: "blessed are the clean of heart"; for those are not "clean of heart" who have not within them blood or any bodily matter. But it was said: "blessed are the clean of heart" in the sense of "blessed" are those who have "a clean heart", the ruling part of the soul being named instead of "heart". Since, therefore, the ruling part of our soul, which is said to be in the bodily "heart", is either "clean" or unclean — and our "heart" is unclean indeed when "the worst thoughts go forth from" it, "murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, blasphemies", but "clean" when there are holy thoughts and divine understandings and a pure mind — on this account it must be judged that it is said to be made thin by the "thin" and holy Spirit of him who is saved, but "thickened" by malice and choked in him who sins. For it is said of the "Holy Spirit", who is according to "wisdom", that he is "only-begotten, manifold, thin, mobile", and that the just man receives this "subtle spirit"; for this "spirit" differs from "all intellectual, clean, subtle spirits". The ruling part of the heart, therefore, is "thin" indeed insofar as it is spiritual, but fat insofar as it is concreted from the vice of bodily matter, full of bodily thoughts, which are under reproach. Thus it is said: "the heart of this people has been thickened". Understand: from this "the heart has been thickened", that there is nothing in it besides human and fleshly cares; for just as the matter of the body is fat, in the same way also are bodily understandings and thoughts. Wherefore, since two things are set before us — that the "heart is thickened" from worldly cares and made thin from spiritual solicitude, when one thinks of the things which are the Lord's, casting off the fatness from the "heart" and knowing that, if his "heart be thickened", he will neither receive the words of God nor see the sacrament of salvation — let us lay aside the thickness and take up that thinness which has been spoken of, so that we too may say, as the prophet: "my soul has thirsted for you; how manifoldly does my flesh thirst for you, in a land desert and pathless and waterless, so in the holy place have I appeared to you" — not as though I were "holy" by nature, but if the prudence "of the flesh" wastes away, and if the prudence "of the flesh" has been wasted, then "in the holy place I shall appear to you". These things in explanation of that which was said: "for the heart of this people has been thickened".

There follows: "and with their ears they have heard heavily". It does me no harm if I "hear heavily" bodily, nor does this become for me a cause that I should not hear the words of God. For just as bodily blindness does me no harm, if my soul has not been blinded, so neither does lightness nor heaviness of bodily hearing hinder me. But there is a certain heaviness of hearing which harms the soul of man. What is this heaviness which is in the hearing of the soul? Sin, according to the scriptures, is "heavy". On which account someone, perceiving his sins, says: "like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me". And because "iniquity" is heavy, on this account "it sits upon a talent of lead", as is written in Zechariah. But the Egyptians "were sunk like lead in the mighty water" not because they had "heavy" bodies, but because their souls "had been made heavy" by the "talent of lead upon which iniquity was sitting" — on this account "they were sunk like lead in the mighty water". The heaviness of "the ears", therefore, comes from sin, and the lightness from righteousness. What is it that makes the hearing "hear" not "heavily", but lightly? The "wings" of the Word, the "wings" of virtue; for indeed the "wings" of the Word bestow much lightness. "Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I shall find rest?" This the prophet says, praying not that he may receive the bodily "wings of a dove", but the "wings of the dove" of the Holy Spirit. And again Solomon says of the rich man: "but he equips for himself wings like an eagle, and he turns back into the house of him who presides over him". If, therefore, we take "wings", we shall hear lightly; but if we sin and are negligent about our wings and our "wings" fall away, we shall be "made heavy" and "shall hear heavily". "With their ears", therefore, the sinners "have heard heavily". All the Jews indeed who then "heard" the Savior "heard" him "heavily", and therefore did not believe. And down to this day, as many as, "hearing" the scriptures, have not "heard" the spiritual word, which is light, but the "letter", which is "heavy" and "kills", "hear heavily". And thus Scripture is heard in a twofold manner: by him who does not understand what is said, it is "heard heavily"; but by him who understands it, it is not only not "heard heavily", but rather keenly, whence one becomes an understanding hearer.

And yet another thing is prophesied about the people of the Jews and about all of us, if we sin. "And they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart". Of those who do not "see", some are "blind" and on account of blindness do not "see"; some are "in darkness" and therefore do not "see"; but others are neither "in darkness" nor blind, but because they "close their eyes" they do not "see". And the divine Scripture knows these differences, which belong to the ruling part of our heart; for the Savior says "to those who are in bonds: come forth, and to those in darkness, that it may be revealed to them", and "to those sitting in the region and shadow of death: a light has arisen for them". These did not "see" for the reason that they were "in darkness", until "a light should arise for them". "Deaf ones, hear, and blind ones, look". These formerly did not "see" for the reason that they were "blind" by nature. But those who are outside these, and who, in comparison with "the blind" and those who are "in darkness", are much worse, are those who do not "see" for the reason that they have willingly "closed their eyes". And that this is so, as we have asserted, the Savior will be a witness to me, saying: "if you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say that you see; your sin remains". And he says well: "you say that you see"; for truly "they say that they see" and have the possibility of "seeing", but, "closing their eyes", they do not "see". And if ever you see a soul ingenious for understanding, and swift and eager, that does not meditate on the words of God, know that it is not on account of blindness that it does not "see" those things which are contained in the scriptures, not because it is "in darkness", but because it "closes its eyes". If, therefore, you have heard Scripture saying to those who "close their eyes": "open your eyes and see rightly", "open your eyes from that which you had closed", then you will be able to "see rightly" and to consider the light of truth. And it accuses indeed those about whom the inquiry is made, why they "close their eyes, lest they see"; yet it does not also say this, that it is never expedient to "close" the "eyes" of the soul. For it is expedient, as Isaiah makes plain, saying in what follows: "who will announce to you the eternal place? He who walks in righteousness and speaks the true and right way, stopping his ears, that he may not hear the judgment of blood, closing his eyes, that he may not see iniquity". If it is going to happen that, opening the "eyes" of my soul, I "hear" and perceive base speech, it is better to "close" the entrances than to "hear" and understand things that harm. When, then, do I "close"? When evil things are spoken, so that I may not even understand them. When the words of God are to be seen, then "we turn back and" God "heals" us, sending the word which "heals" those who wish to be cured in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

Let us examine what this means, which is said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat". Everyone who is occupied in the cares of the present life has "a heart made fat"; for those who dwell among worldly things the "heart is made fat" no otherwise than as if they were being choked by thorns. For this reason the "heart" grows fat and cannot receive the notions of the more subtle spirit. Let us therefore flee from such cares, so that our heart, made thin, may become acceptable to God. Let us flee earthly business; for these are the things by which the "heart is made fat". On account of this the discourse of Moses was subtle (as is written of him in Exodus), because he said that whoever, on account of such subtlety, shall be "pure in heart, they shall see God". For by such eyes God is seen. There are three things that are said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat" and "with their ears they have heard heavily" and "they have closed their eyes". But the things said in this passage can also be understood otherwise, more plainly. For many people think, when they look upon the creatures and contemplate this world, that they see them. And why do I speak of people? Behold, the birds and the four-footed beasts see the sun and the moon and the whole heaven together with the choir of stars, but they do not understand their reasons; only the just and holy, comprehending them through the reason of the wisdom of God, look upon them. Therefore in the eighth Psalm David says: "for I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded". For does the prophet not now "see the heaven and the moon"? But this, that he says: "I shall see", if we consider it, we shall be able to understand.

For the heart of this people has grown fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes, and the rest. He gives the reasons why seeing they do not see and hearing they do not hear: because it has grown fat, he says, the heart of this people, and with their ears they have heard heavily; and lest perhaps we should think that fatness of heart and heaviness of ears belong to nature, not to the will, he adds the fault of free choice and says: They have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and be converted, and I should heal them. In parables, therefore, and in an enigma do they hear who, with their eyes closed, do not wish to see the truth.

Behold mercy and judgment: mercy upon the elect, who have obtained the justice of God, but judgment upon the others who have been blinded. And yet the former have believed, because they have willed, while the latter have not believed, because they have not willed. Hence mercy and judgment were brought about in their own wills. Clearly this election is through grace, not at all through merits.

But the words of the Gospel also, that follow, are still more pressing, and start a question of more profound import: for He goes on to say, "Therefore they could not believe, because that Isaiah said again, He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them." For it is said to us: If they could not believe, what sin is it in man not to do what he cannot do and if they sinned in not believing, then they had the power to believe, and did not use it. If, then, they had the power, how says the Gospel, "Therefore they could not believe, because that Isaiah said again, He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart;" so that (which is of grave import) to God Himself is referred the cause of their not believing, inasmuch as it is He who "hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart"? For what is thus testified to in the prophetical Scriptures, is at least not spoken of the devil, but of God. For were we to suppose it said of the devil, that he "hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart;" we have to undertake the task of being able to show what blame was theirs in not believing, of whom it is said, "they could not believe." And then, what reply shall we give touching another testimony of this very prophet, which the Apostle Paul has adopted, when he says: "Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it, and the rest were blinded, according as it is written, God hath given them the spirit of remorse, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, unto this day"?

Such, as you have just heard, brethren, is the question that comes before us, and you can perceive how profound it is; but we shall give what answer we can. "They could not believe," because that Isaiah the prophet foretold it; and the prophet foretold it because God foreknew that such would be the case. But if I am asked why they could not, I reply at once, because they would not; for certainly their depraved will was foreseen by God, and foretold through the prophet by Him from whom nothing that is future can be hid. But the prophet, sayest thou, assigns another cause than that of their will. What cause does the prophet assign? That "God hath given them the spirit of remorse, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear; and hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart." This also, I reply, their will deserved. For God thus blinds and hardens, simply by letting alone and withdrawing His aid: and God can do this by a judgment that is hidden, although not by one that is unrighteous. This is a doctrine which the piety of the God-fearing ought to preserve unshaken and inviolable in all its integrity: even as the apostle, when treating of the same intricate question, says, "What shall we say then? is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid." If, then, we must be far from thinking that there is unrighteousness with God, this only can it be,that, when He giveth His aid, He acteth mercifully; and, when He withholdeth it, He acteth righteously: for in all He doeth, He acteth not rashly, but in accordance with judgment. And still further, if the judgments of the saints are righteous, how much more those of the sanctifying and justifying God? They are therefore righteous, although hidden. Accordingly, when questions of this sort come before us, why one is dealt with in such a way, and another in such another way; why this one is blinded by being forsaken of God, and that one is enlightened by the divine aid vouchsafed to him: let us not take upon ourselves to pass judgment on the judgment of so mighty a judge, but tremblingly exclaim with the apostle, "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out!" As it is also said in the psalm, "Thy judgments are as a great deep."

But when he added, "And they should be converted, and I should heal them," is there a "not" to be understood, that is, they should not be converted, connecting it with the clause before, where it is said, "that they should not see with their eyes and understand with their heart;" for here also it is certainly meant, "and should not understand "? For conversion itself is likewise a gift of His grace, as when it is said to Him, "Turn us, O God of Hosts." Or may it be that we are to understand this also as actually taking place through the merciful experience of the divine method of healing, [namely this,] that, being of proud and perverse wills, and wishing to establish their own righteousness, they were left alone for the very purpose of being blinded; and thus blinded in order that they might stumble on the stone of stumbling, and have their faces filled with shame; and so, being thus humbled, might seek the name of the Lord, and no longer a righteousness of their own, that inflated their pride, but the righteousness of God, that justifieth the ungodly? For this very way turned out to the good of many of them, who were afterwards filled with remorse for wickedness, and believed on Christ; and on whose behalf He Himself had put up the prayer, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." And it is of that ignorance of theirs also that the apostle says, "I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge:" for he then goes on also to add, "For they, being ignorant of God's righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God."

228. Second, the acceptance of the sentence is set out. And these are the words of prophet; hence he says: O Lord, from that by which the Gentiles shall come in, strike Israel with blindness (Rom 11:25): blind the heart, inwardly, and make their ears heavy, lest they perceive, and shut their eyes, lest they understand: for judgment I am come into this world: that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind (John 9:39). Or these are the words of the Lord, and the sense is: blind, that is, proclaim them blind.

Third, the reason for their blindness is set out: lest, for the sake of goods, they be converted and I heal them, when they are unworthy of health: but if the wicked do penance for all his sins which he has committed, and keep all my commandments, and do judgment, and justice, living he shall live, and shall not die. I will not remember all his iniquities (Ezek 18:21–22), below: if you return and be quiet, you shall be saved (Isa 30:15).

And I said: How long, Lord? And he said: Until the cities are made desolate without inhabitant, and the houses without men, and the land is left deserted. And the Lord will remove men far away, and she that had been forsaken in the midst of the land shall be multiplied. And yet in it there shall be a tithing, and again it shall be for a plundering, like a terebinth, and like an oak that has cast its fruits: the seed that shall have stood in it shall be holy. The Lord says: Go, and tell this people that it hears and does not hear, sees and does not see. And for this reason it neither hears nor sees: because it is not going to understand the words of the Lord nor to recognize his works, and because it has grown fat and broad and has forgotten its Creator (Deut 32). The Prophet answers, and asks anxiously about his people: How long, Lord, will this sentence remain, that hearing it should not hear, and seeing should not see? To whom the Lord answered: So long will it not hear and not see, and have its heart blinded, until the cities of Judea, when Vespasian and Titus make war, are utterly overthrown, so much so that not even their former name remains, and the houses, if any remain, are without inhabitant, and the land is reduced to a wilderness; and the Jewish people is scattered over the whole world, either by flight or by captivity; and the people of the Jews is multiplied no longer in Judea, as before, but among all the nations.

229. And I said. Here the length of the sentence is set out.

And first, the question of the prophet is set out: how long will they be blinded? How long shall the vision . . . be trodden under foot? (Dan 8:13);

second, the answer of the Lord: and he said.

And a twofold ending is set out:

first, as to the punishment of the wicked,

second as to the holiness of the good, where it says, a holy seed (Isa 6:13), as if to say: how long will those who are in filth be filthy? He that hurts, let him hurt still: and he that is filthy, let him be filthy still (Rev 22:11).

And he touches on a threefold punishment.

First, as to subjugation, which is designated in the desolation of their cities: until the cities be wasted: they have changed my delightful portion into a desolate wilderness (Jer 12:10); he has made me desolate, wasted with sorrow all the day long (Lam 1:13); as to the cultivation of their fields: the land shall be left desolate, above: your land is desolate, your cities are burnt with fire (Isa 1:7).

229 [cont.]. As to the exile of men: and the Lord shall remove men far away: and I will send you, and your mother that bore you, into a strange country, in which you were not born, and there you shall die (Jer 22:26). And I will pick out from among you the transgressors, and the wicked, and will bring them out of the land where they sojourn (Ezek 20:38).

230. Second, as to the length of their captivity: and she shall be multiplied, that people, that was left in the midst of the land, in which she will be held captive: thus says the Lord of hosts the God of Israel, to all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: build houses, and dwell in them (Jer 29:4–5), and below this: and be multiplied there, and be not few in number. And seek the peace of the city, to which I have caused you to be carried away (Jer 29:6–7).

But also even after the departure of those who are clearly the apostles of our Saviour, he says that "a tenth" will still remain on Jewish soil:

"And again it shall be for a spoil, as a terebinth, and as an acorn, when it falls out of its husk."

The Scripture, as I suppose, means by this, that after the first siege, which they are recorded to have undergone in the time of the apostles, and of Vespasian, Emperor of the Romans, being a second time besieged again under Hadrian they were completely debarred from entering the place, so that they were not even allowed to tread the soil of Jerusalem. And this he darkly suggests in the words : "And again it shall be for a spoil, as a terebinth, and as an acorn when it falls out of its husk "
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

And though I say that it is multiplied, so great will be the misfortune of the remnant of the people that, in comparison with its former multitude, scarcely a tenth part remains. And when there is a wilderness in the land itself also (for this place can be understood in two ways: that scarcely a tenth part remains even in the whole world, and that in Judea itself scarcely a small part of the people is preserved), again those very remnants will be for a plundering, when, after about fifty years, Hadrian comes and has utterly plundered the land of Judea, so much so that it is compared to a terebinth and to an oak that has lost its acorns. Finally, after the last devastation, public laws were even posted, and the Jews were forbidden to enter the land from which they had been cast out. But if anyone believes in Christ, and that is fulfilled which we read above: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9): when, according to the Apostle (Rom 9), the remnant will be saved; this seed will be holy, and from the shoot of the Apostles all the Churches will sprout. What we have said, the seed that shall have stood in it shall be holy, or according to Aquila, its shoot shall be a holy seed, is not found in the Seventy Translators, but was added by Origen from the Hebrew and the edition of Theodotion; it is carried in the copies of the Church, so that after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel may be saved; and that in this too the word of the Lord may be fulfilled, who says: I will kill, and I will make alive, and I will strike, and I will heal (Deut 32:39).
7: And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah: Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, the king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight against it, and they could not subdue it. And they told the house of David, saying: Syria has come to an agreement with Ephraim; and his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the woods are moved before the wind. Uzziah, who is also Azariah, king of Judah, reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years (2 Kgs 15). At the very end of his time Isaiah saw the things which the preceding discourse has set out. When he was dead and Jotham his son, a most righteous king, was reigning in his place, the prophet at once saw the Lord and Savior reigning in his majesty, and announcing the blindness of the Jewish people, and the overthrow of Jerusalem and of the other cities under Vespasian and Hadrian; and how in the Apostles a remnant was to be saved. As third king, the son of Jotham, Ahaz succeeds, a most impious man (2 Kgs 16; 2 Chr 28), who shut the doors of the temple, and in the valley of Ben-hinnom worshipped the Baals, and consecrated his son to idols; so that he even took away the bronze altar that Solomon had made, and placed in the Temple of God an altar of the idols, whose pattern he had received from Damascus. Justly, therefore, was he forsaken by the help of the Lord, and Rezin the king of Syria, that is, Aram, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel in Samaria, rose up together against him, and came to Jerusalem to storm it (ibid.). We read in the book of Chronicles that Rezin the king of Damascus, having conquered Ahaz, carried many from Judea off to Damascus; and that Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of the ten tribes, which were called Israel, who reigned in Samaria, struck down in one day a hundred and twenty thousand fighting men of Judah, and led captive into Samaria two hundred thousand women, boys and girls, with boundless plunder. Of that contest the prophet has now kept silent, but relates the second battle, when, having had proof of their strength and victory, and lured by the greatness of the plunder, they come again to Judea and desire to subdue Jerusalem, and could not, because the Lord helped it, so that, on the occasion of the mercy by which he was freeing the besieged people, he might announce that his Son would be born of a Virgin. When the house of David, that is, the royal house, heard that Syria and Ephraim, that is, Rezin and Pekah, were coming with joined army, it was terrified and greatly afraid, and both king and people trembled so that you would think the leaves of trees were being tossed by the blasts of the winds. According to the anagogy the interpretation is easy: that while Ahaz the impious king is reigning, the king of Aram, which is interpreted lofty and sublime, so as to indicate the arrogance of secular wisdom, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, who himself too, according to the prophet Hosea, was of the tribe of Ephraim, from which Jeroboam the son of Nebat had set up the golden calves in Bethel and Dan (1 Kgs 12) and had separated the people of God from David, are referred to the heretics, who agree together to storm the Church. And when the house of David hears this, David whom we read in Ezekiel is to be raised up as the good shepherd (Ezek 34), and his people believing simply in the Lord, it trembles greatly. And it trembles for this reason, because it is compared not to fruit-bearing trees but to an unfruitful forest. And that these same heretics and the gentiles fight against the house of David with the swords of arguments and of the dialectical art, no one doubts: so that those who are at variance among themselves agree in attacking the Church; according to that instance in which Herod and Pilate, who were at discord with each other, were bound together in friendship at the Lord's passion.

And it came to pass in the days of Achaz the son of Joathan. Here the threat against the enemies of the two tribes is set out. And it is divided into two parts: in the first, the threat against the persecutors of the people is set out; in the second, the threat against those who are contemptuous of the prophecies of the prophets: woe to the crown of pride (ch. 28). The first of these is divided into two: in the first, the overthrow of each enemy in particular; in the second, of all of them in general: behold the Lord shall lay waste the earth (ch. 24). The first of these is divided into three: in the first, against enemies who persecute them bodily; in the second, against enemies who furnish power: the burden of Damascus (ch. 17); in the third, against enemies who oppress them in things: the burden of the desert of the sea (ch. 21). The first of these is divided into two: in the first, against persecutors of the same nation; in the second, against foreign persecutors: woe to them that make wicked laws (ch. 10). The first of these is divided into two: in the first, he threatens the frustration of the impious through the liberation of the two tribes; in the second, their destruction: and the Lord said to me (ch. 8). The first part, which is contained in this chapter, is divided into three: in the first, the imminent danger is described; in the second, the benefit of liberation is promised: and the Lord said to Isaiah (Isa 7:3); in the third, the sign of liberation is conferred, where it says, and the Lord spoke again to Achaz (Isa 7:10).

To understand the first part, it should be known that Achaz was impious and an idolater, as we read in 2 Kings 16:2–4 and 2 Chronicles 27; and therefore, the Lord gave him into the hand of the kings of Syria and Samaria, who first came against him and, besieging Jerusalem and finally conquering it, captured the greater part of his army and the chief of his army. Confident from that victory, they came again to deprive him of the kingdom entirely, and substitute another in his place. And in this second coming, Isaiah consoled him.

Three things, therefore, are set out in the first part. First, the gathering of the enemies is described; hence he says: and it came to pass in the days of Achaz. And he takes the genealogy back to Ozias, perhaps because it was when Ozias was struck with leprosy by the Lord (2 Chr 26:19–23), though he had once been just, that they received the daring to invade as though disdaining divine help. Came up, this is said because of the position of the land, for Judah is in the mountains; Phacee, who killed Phaceia king of Israel, whose chief of military he was, and reigned in his place; but they could not prevail over it, the first time, although they conquered the king in the battlefield. Or this is said by anticipation, as to the second time they came up.

Second, he sets out the declaration of this: and they, his scouts, told the house of David, that is, the royal house, saying: Syria has rested upon Ephraim, that is, the king of Syria with the king of the ten tribes, which are called Ephraim, because of their first king, who belonged to the tribe of Ephraim (1 Kings 13) or because of honor; they were joined in friendship although they were formerly enemies, as is read in 1 Kings 22. And he says, Syria has rested upon Ephraim, that it be noted that the kingdom of Syria held the first place in the alliance, because it was stronger.

Third, the effect of the declaration is set out, namely disturbance of the king and his people: and his, namely, the king's, heart was moved, and the heart of his people: so also a fearful heart in the thought of a fool (Sir 22:23); and dread to them that work iniquity (Prov 21:15); and king Herod hearing this, was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matt 2:3).

This much we have said according to the history. But according to the tropology we have begun, we must consider that Isaiah is ordered to meet the impious king, going out from his own place, not at the beginning of the conduit, but at the outermost bounds of the upper pool, which was in the fuller's field, where filth and stains were washed away. For although Ahaz was reigning over Judah, yet because he was impious he lingered at the outermost bounds of the upper pool. So God has mercy not so much on the king, whom he judged unworthy of salvation, as on his people. And by the two tails of smoking brands, as we said before, he means secular wisdom and heretical speech, whose end is burning. They took counsel in vain to go up against Judah, and to seize it as though negligent and sleeping, and to join it to their own errors, and to set over it as king the son of Tabeel, that is, of the good God. For each adversary judges that the truth is with himself, that the best doctrine is with himself. Indeed Marcion the heretic thinks that Christ is the son of the good God, that is, of another, and not of the just God whose the Prophets are, whom he calls bloodthirsty, cruel, and a judge. While they say these things, the Lord threatens that their counsel shall not stand, but that for the meantime, now, as long as this world stands, the things also that are of the world hold sway within their own bounds and in their own cities. But when the time of the consummation has come, that is, the sixty-five years, and both the things of the world, which were made in six days, and all that pertains to the five senses have received their end, then all things are to be dissolved, which the gentiles and the heretics do not believe will come, and on account of their unbelief they do not understand the things that are said.

And the Lord said to Isaiah: Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Jasub your son who is left, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field. And you shall say to him: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and let not your heart be afraid of the two tails of these smoking firebrands, in the wrath of the fury of Rezin and of Syria and of the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah have taken most evil counsel against you, saying: Let us go up to Judah, and rouse it up, and tear it away to ourselves, and set a king in the midst of it, the son of Tabeel. Thus says the Lord God: It shall not stand, and this shall not be; but the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin, and yet sixty-five years, and Ephraim shall cease to be a people. And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria the son of Remaliah. If you do not believe, you shall not remain. Jasub the son of Isaiah, which is interpreted left over and returning, as a type of the people of Judah, which was to be freed from the hands of two kings, is ordered to go out with his father and to meet Ahaz king of Judah at the place of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field, where we shall read later that under Hezekiah king of Judah Rabshakeh stood and, at the command of Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, blasphemed the people of God. To which place there went out, sent by Hezekiah, the princes of the city whom we read of in the volume of Kings.

And let it not disturb anyone that we take the pool in the bad sense, when that pool to which Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, is commanded to go up is taken in the good sense. For there it is said with an addition: The pool of the aqueduct, and the pool of the fuller, which is accustomed to wash away filth and to cleanse the stains of garments. And because it is set on high, the prophet is therefore commanded to go up to it and, in meeting the king, to promise victory over the two burnt firebrands.

And the Lord said to Isaiah. Here liberation is promised. And first, the manner of the promise is set out; second, the promise itself: and you shall say to him (Isa 7:4). And the manner is set out first, as to the person announcing it: the Lord said to Isaiah, inspiring him inwardly, or speaking through a subordinate creature: go forth to meet Achaz, who perhaps because of fear of the enemy had gone to prepare himself to resist.

Second, as to the witness: and Jasub your son that is left, to you, the other brother, namely, Rabsaces, who was born from a more noble mother, having fled to the king of the Assyrians, because he was not received well by Achaz: about whom, see below (Isa 36:2); in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand (Deut 19:15).

Third, as to the place, to the end. To understand this, it should be known that because Jerusalem is in the mountains, it does not abound in flowing waters, and therefore, they had water in pools, collected either from the rain or from remote springs via aqueducts. Now there were three pools in Jerusalem: one which was for the use of the priests and sacrifices, which was called the Probatica pool, about which, see John 5:2; the second was lower in the city and was kept clean for the general use of the city; the third was outside the city and had unclean water; in it fullers would wash wool, and it was for this kind of use: and from that pool is named the whole fuller's field. And thus is made clear what is said in the text.

And Ahaz (2 Kgs 18), though an impious king, is commanded, on account of the mercy of the Lord, to keep silence and not to be terrified, nor let his heart be afraid, thinking that he will suffer things like those he had endured before. And he calls Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Samaria two tails of firebrands, that is, of smoking brands, because in them the kingdom of Syria, that is, of Damascus, was ended, and the kingdom of Samaria, that is, of the ten tribes, which by another name were called Ephraim. For it is written (2 Kgs 16) that Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, under king Ahaz, went up against Damascus and laid it waste, and carried its inhabitants off to Kir, and killed Rezin; and that Hoshea the son of Elah laid an ambush for Pekah the son of Remaliah, and struck him and killed him, and reigned in his place in Israel nine years; and that Shalmaneser king of Assyria came and besieged Samaria, which is now called Sebaste, for three years, and in the ninth year of the reign of Hoshea took it, and sent Hoshea bound into prison, and carried Israel off to the Assyrians, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river Gozan, in the cities, or, as the Seventy translated, in the mountains of the Medes (2 Kgs 17).

And you shall say to him. Here he sets out the promise: and first, he sets out strengthening; second, the reason for strengthening: of the two tails of these firebrands; third, the condemnation of the unbelieving, where it says, if you will not believe, you shall not continue (Isa 7:9).

And he strengthens them, prohibiting the sign of fear: see you be quiet, that is, beware lest you outwardly reveal the fear of your heart, below: in silence and in hope shall your strength be (Isa 30:15), and in the same place: and the work of justice shall be peace, and the service of justice quietness, and security for ever (Isa 32:17). And he also shows the passage of fear: fear not, the evils to come, and let not your heart be afraid, because of the memory of the evils which you have suffered, below: fear not, for I am with you: I will bring your seed from the east, and gather you from the west (Isa 43:5).

Of the two tails. Here he sets out the reason for strengthening. And first, he shows the vanity of the proposers, who propose great things, though they can sustain nothing or very little: the two tails, because the kingdom was ended in them. For Rasin was killed by Theglathphalasar (2 Kings 16:9), and led his people into captivity; but Phacee was made subject, and afterwards was killed by an enemy, who a little later was captured by Salmanasar, and the ten tribes were taken captive (2 Kings 17:3–6). Smoking: for they were then near to being extinguished.

For although these two most evil kings took counsel to go up to Judah, whose region is set in the mountains, and to rouse it up while it was at rest and in a manner sleeping, and to subjugate it to their own rule, and to set over it as king the son of Tabeel, which is interpreted good God, so as to indicate either a man of this name or an idol; nevertheless thus says the Lord God: This counsel shall not stand, but for the meantime only Damascus shall be the head of the cities of Syria, and in Damascus itself, the metropolis, Rezin shall rule. Further, in Ephraim, on account of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who first reigned from Ephraim, Samaria shall be the head, that is, the royal house in the city of Samaria, and the head of Samaria shall be the son of Remaliah, that is, Pekah; but the kingdom of the ten tribes, that is, of the people of Ephraim, will cease to exist after sixty-five years. Which, unless we attend more carefully, cannot stand. For in the twelfth year of Ahaz the son of Jotham in the tribe of Judah, Hoshea reigned over Samaria, and in the ninth year of his rule he was taken (2 Kgs 17). And Ahaz reigned over Judah sixteen years (2 Kgs 16), and in the seventh year of Hoshea's rule after Ahaz's death Hoshea was taken, and Samaria destroyed, and the whole people carried over into Media: so that if we choose to put sixteen years of Ahaz and seven of Hoshea, the result is twenty-three years, or at most twenty-four; and where will the sixty-five years be, within which the kingdom of Israel is said to be ended? The Hebrews therefore set out this place thus: that Amos, who began to prophesy under Uzziah, when Isaiah too had the beginning of his prophecy, was the first to prophesy against Israel, saying: But Israel shall be led captive out of his land (Amos 7:11, 17). And that the title of his prophecy is against Samaria; and that he began to prophesy in the days of Uzziah king of Judah two years before the earthquake, which they hold to have occurred at the time when Uzziah, entering the Temple of God, claimed the priesthood for himself, and the earth was struck, and the ashes of the altar were poured out, and the king himself was struck with leprosy (2 Chr 26). And they hold that it was the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah when these things happened, whose remaining years are twenty-seven. For Uzziah reigned fifty-two years (2 Kgs 15); after him reigned Jotham his son for sixteen years, and his son Ahaz for another sixteen years; after whom reigned Hezekiah, in the sixth year of whose rule Samaria was taken; and thus sixty-five years are made up together (2 Kgs 16).
Rouse it up, like someone resting in sleep, and draw it away, that is, let us draw it into our power. The son of Tabeel, literally, a certain man, or an idol of our god; Tabeel means "God is good."

Second, as to the frustration of the proposal: thus says the Lord, who can do all things, this shall not be, because it will not be carried into effect, and it shall not stand, because they will not last long in such a proposal, with greater evils rushing in upon them, below: take counsel together, and it shall be defeated: speak a word, and it shall not be done: because God is with us (Isa 8:10).

Know moreover, beloved, that there is no law for God. For sometimes He increases and diminishes, and sometimes He adds to because it is little. For in the days of Noah on account of the sins of men He promised that the days of men should be one hundred and twenty years, and in the six hundredth year of the years of the life of Noah He destroyed them. For He said: "A hundred and twenty years they shall be upon the earth." And in the six hundredth year of the years of the life of Noah they were destroyed, and he took away these twenty years. And again it is written that when iniquity increased the sins of the house of Ephraim, when Jeroboam ruled over them, the son of Nebat, that he sinned and caused Israel to sin, and when they sinned He promised in their behalf by the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet, who said to them that after sixty-five years He will cut off Ephraim from the people. This word was in the first year of Ahaz, and in the fourth year of Hezekiah Shalmanasar, King of Assyria ('Ôtûr), came up against them, and after him Taglathphalasar, and he carried them into exile from their land. For Ahaz reigned over them sixteen years, and in the fourth year of Hezekiah the kings of Assyria ruled over them; so there were only twenty years and He cut off Ephraim from the people of Israel, and He took away from them forty-five years, and this time which at first He had appointed He did not complete according to that which He had decreed.

Third, as to the destruction of the enemies; and first, as to the Assyrians: but the head of Syria, as if to say: but in the meantime, and before they are destroyed, the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rasin, as if to say: the Damascenes and their king will be contained in their borders. And within threescore and five years, Ephraim shall cease to be a people, because they will be taken captive. These years should not be computed from the time of this prophecy, but from the time when Ozias was struck with leprosy, because it was then that they received the daring to invade, in the twenty-sixth year of his reign. And from that time Joathan his son reigned twenty-seven years, while his father still lived, and afterwards sixteen years; then Achaz reigned sixteen years, and then Ezechias, in the sixth year of whose reign, the people were taken captive (2 Kings 17:5). And these taken together are sixty-five years.

And quite necessarily the prophet prefaces Christ's Birth of a Virgin by an exhortation to attention, crying aloud to his hearers, "If ye will not believe, neither shall ye understand."

And then he adds the following words:

"10. And the Lord added to speak unto Ahaz saying, 11. Ask for thyself a sign from the Lord thy God in the depth or in the height. 12. And Ahaz said, I will not ask, neither will I tempt God. 13. And he said, Hear now, house of David; is it a small thing to you to strive with man, and how do ye strive with the Lord? 14. Therefore the Lord shall give you a sign: Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and thou shalt call his name Emmanuel: 15. Butter and honey shall he eat, before he knows to choose the good and refuse the evil. 16. Wherefore before the child know good or evil, he does not obey wickedness, that he should choose the good. And the earth shall be forsaken, on account of that which thou fearest, of her two kings."

Such is the prophecy. But the opening of the prophecy is worthy of our study, which bears witness to those that read it, "If ye do not believe, neither will ye understand." And it is above all necessary to note that the words shew that its readers need not only intellect but faith, and not only faith but intellect. Hence the Jews who do not believe in Christ, though they are even now hearers of these words, have not even yet understood Him of Whom the prophecy was given, so that in their case the prediction has its primary fulfilment. For though they hear daily with their ears the prophecies about Christ, they hear them not with the ears of their mind. And the sole cause of their ignorance is unbelief, as the prophecy truly reveals of them and to them. For it says, "If ye will not believe, neither shall ye understand."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 1

Certainly one must have faith in the Scriptures as containing the divine mind, and thus one must proceed to the understanding of what is written in them. For one must go beyond the types and thus apprehend the truth of what has been shown to us. First one must believe in the Scriptures with the simple faith that they are "inspired by God and useful" and then go on to examine subtly and enquiringly the meaning contained in them.

That the way to understand, therefore, may be open to you, you do rightly first of all, in professing that you believe; for no one embarks upon the sea and trusts himself to the deep and liquid element unless he first believes it possible that he will have a safe voyage. Neither does the husbandman commit his seed to the furrows and scatter his grain on the earth, but in the belief that the showers will come, together with the sun's warmth, through whose fostering influence, aided by favoring winds, the earth will produce and multiply and ripen its fruits. Nothing in life can be transacted if there be not first a readiness to believe. What wonder then, if, coming to God, we first of all profess that we believe, seeing that, without this, not even common life can be lived.

When the Lord foretold these things through the prophet, both Ahaz and the people did not believe that they would come to pass. Hence it is added: If you do not believe, you shall not remain, as Symmachus translated, that is, you too shall not remain in your kingdom, but shall be led into captivity, suffering the penalties of those whose unbelief you have imitated. Or certainly, according to the Seventy, you shall not understand. And the sense is: because you do not believe the things that the Lord says are to come, you will not have understanding.

The commandments are those concerning righteousness, and the righteousness is that which is by faith, surrounded with the uncertainty of temptations; so that understanding is the reward of a pious belief of what is not yet understood. The meaning I have given to these words, "Thou hast desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord shall give it thee," I find also in the passage, "Unless ye believe, ye shall not understand;" showing that as righteousness is by faith, understanding comes by wisdom. Accordingly, in the case of those who eagerly demand evident truth, we must not condemn the desire, but regulate it, so that beginning with faith it may proceed to the desired end through good works. The life of virtue is one of toil; the end desired is unclouded wisdom.
If you are not able to understand, believe, that you may understand. Faith goes before; understanding follows after; since the prophet says, "Unless you believe, you shall not understand.

The mysteries and secrets of the kingdom of God first seek for believing people, that they may make them understanding. For faith is understanding's step, and understanding faith's attainment. This the prophet expressly says to all who prematurely and in undue order look for understanding and neglect faith.

So, then, in some points that bear on the doctrine of salvation, which we are not yet able to grasp by reason—but we shall be able to sometime—let faith precede reason, and let the heart be cleansed by faith so as to receive and bear the great light of reason; this is indeed reasonable. Therefore the prophet said with reason: "If you will not believe, you will not understand"; thereby he undoubtedly made a distinction between these two things and advised us to believe first so as to be able to understand whatever we believe. It is, then, a reasonable requirement that faith precede reason, for, if this requirement is not reasonable, then it is contrary to reason, which God forbid. But, if it is reasonable that faith precede a certain great reason that cannot yet be grasped, there is no doubt that, however slight the reason which proves this, it does precede faith.

If we have understood this, thanks be to God; but if any has not sufficiently understood, man has done as far as he could: as for the rest, let him see whence he may hope to understand. As laborers outside, we can plant and water; but it is of God to give the increase. "My doctrine," saith He, "is not mine, but His that sent me." Let him who says he has not yet understood hear counsel. For since it was a great and profound matter that had been spoken, the Lord Christ Himself did certainly see that all would not understand this so profound a matter, and He gave counsel in the sequel. Dost thou wish to understand? Believe. For God has said by the prophet: "Except ye believe, ye shall not understand." To the same purpose what the Lord here also added as He went on"If any man is willing to do His will, he shall know concerning the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak from myself." What is the meaning of this, "If any man be willing to do His will"? But I had said, if any man believe; and I gave this counsel: If thou hast not understood, said I, believe. For understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that thou mayest understand; since, "except ye believe, ye shall not understand." Therefore when I would counsel the obedience of believing toward the possibility of understanding, and say that our Lord Jesus Christ has added this very thing in the following sentence, we find Him to have said, "If any man be willing to do His will, he shall know of the doctrine." What is "he shall know"? It is the same thing as "he shall understand." But what is "If any man be willing to do His will"? It is the same thing as to believe. All men indeed perceive that "shall know" is the same thing as "shall understand:" but that the saying, "If any man be willing to do His will," refers to believing, all do not perceive; to perceive this more accurately, we need the Lord Himself for expounder, to show us whether the doing of the Father's will does in reality refer to believing. But who does not know that this is to do the will of God, to work the work of God; that is, to work that work which is pleasing to Him? But the Lord Himself says openly in another place: "This is the work of God, that ye believe on Him whom He has sent." "That ye believe on Him," not, that ye believe Him. But if ye believe on Him, ye believe Him; yet he that believes Him does not necessarily believe on Him. For even the devils believed Him, but they did not believe on Him. Again, moreover, of His apostles we can say, we believe Paul; but not, we believe on Paul: we believe Peter; but not, we believe on Peter. For, "to him that believeth on Him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted unto him for righteousness." What then is "to believe on Him"? By believing to love Him, by believing to esteem highly, by believing to go into Him and to be incorporated in His members. It is faith itself then that God exacts from us: and He finds not that which He exacts, unless He has bestowed what He may find. What faith, but that which the apostle has most amply defined in another place, saying, "Neither circumcision availeth anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith that worketh by love?" Not any faith of what kind soever, but "faith that worketh by love:" let this faith be in thee, and thou shall understand concerning the doctrine. What indeed shall thou understand? That "this doctrine is not mine, but His that sent me;" that is, thou shall understand that Christ the Son of God, who is the doctrine of the Father, is not from Himself, but is the Son of the Father.

If however any more subtle inference of man's argumentation and reasoning seems opposed to this interpretation, it should be avoided rather than brought forward to the destruction of the faith (for we gain not faith from understanding, but understanding from faith, as it is written: "Except ye believe, ye will not understand" ) for how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.
The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 18

Isaiah according to the Septuagint translation says: "Unless you believe, you shall not understand." And Augustine says: "Unless a man captivates his understanding and follows through faith what he hears, he is not disposed to the gift of understanding." A man is disposed to receive worthily the gift of understanding through the captivation of the intelligence. He who wishes to search sacred Scripture according to the light of his own intelligence thinks the most false errors. In this life we are little ones, and "the learner must believe." For it is necessary to believe God, and especially in sublime matters that transcend our understanding. The first Angel erred because he presumed upon himself.

There is no salvation except through wisdom. But wisdom is neither disclosed nor obtained except through faith. Hence: "Unless you believe, you shall not understand." For you should not "be more wise than it behooveth to be wise,... according as God hath divided to every one the measure of faith." For faith is not had except through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

And the head of Ephraim, as above.

If you will not believe. Here he places the condemnation of the unbelieving. If you will not believe, namely in the promises of the Lord, you too shall not continue in your land, but you will be taken captive: behold, he that is unbelieving, his soul shall not be right in himself (Hab 2:4). And he says this because Achaz, not believing the prophecy, called upon the support of the king of Assyrians, Theglathphalasar, that he might help him; Theglathphalasar came at his petition and destroyed Damascus and killed its king; and though he had given him tribute, nevertheless it profited him nothing, as is said in 2 Chronicles 28:21.

For the one and the same Spirit of God, who proclaimed by the prophets what and of what sort the advent of the Lord should be, did by these elders give a just interpretation of what had been truly prophesied; and He did Himself, by the apostles, announce that the fulness of the times of the adoption had arrived, that the kingdom of heaven had drawn nigh, and that He was dwelling within those that believe on Him who was born Emmanuel of the Virgin. To this effect they testify, [saying,] that before Joseph had come together with Mary, while she therefore remained in virginity, "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost;" [Matthew 1:18] and that the angel Gabriel said unto her, "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God;" [Luke 1:35] and that the angel said to Joseph in a dream, "Now this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, Behold, a virgin shall be with child." [Matthew 1:23] But the elders have thus interpreted what Esaias said: "And the Lord, moreover, said unto Ahaz, Ask for thyself a sign from the Lord thy God out of the depth below, or from the height above. And Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord. And he said, It is not a small thing for you to weary men; and how does the Lord weary them? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son; and ye shall call His name Emmanuel. Butter and honey shall He eat: before He knows or chooses out things that are evil, He shall exchange them for what is good; for before the child knows good or evil, He shall not consent to evil, that He may choose that which is good." [Isaiah 7:10-17] Carefully, then, has the Holy Ghost pointed out, by what has been said, His birth from a virgin, and His essence, that He is God (for the name Emmanuel indicates this). And He shows that He is a man, when He says, "Butter and honey shall He eat;" and in that He terms Him a child also, [in saying,] "before He knows good and evil;" for these are all the tokens of a human infant. But that He "will not consent to evil, that He may choose that which is good,"— this is proper to God; that by the fact, that He shall eat butter and honey, we should not understand that He is a mere man only, nor, on the other hand, from the name Emmanuel, should suspect Him to be God without flesh.

And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell, or in the height above. He who had before spoken to Ahaz through the prophet: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and the rest, since Ahaz did not believe and therefore did not understand, himself speaks to Ahaz: that, terrified at least by the authority of the Lord, he may accept what is said. Because it seems difficult to you, he says, that most powerful kingdoms are to be ended in a short time, and that you with your people should be freed from great danger, ask for yourself a sign, not at all from the idols in whose error you are held, but from the Lord your God, who promises you help; and the very sign is of your own choosing, whence you would demand it, whether from the depth or from the height. Whereas the Seventy alone said this, the others, according to the Hebrew, translated more expressively, from the depth of hell. So just as the depth signifies hell, so by the height we ought to understand above the heavens: so that when you have received a sign from hell or from the height, you may believe that the things I have said will come. Do you wish, he says, that the earth be split, and that the underworld, which is said to be in the heart of the earth, lie open with a great gaping; or that the heavens be opened? Both of which pertain to the type of the Lord's death and ascension: For he who descended is the same who also ascended (Eph 4:10). And in the Apostle we read: Do not say in your heart, Who has ascended into heaven? that is, to bring Christ down. Or, Who has descended into the abyss? that is, to bring Christ back from the dead (Rom 10:6-7). And in another place, disputing about Christ, he says: What is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth of the surpassing knowledge and love of Christ (Eph 3:18). This, so far as concerns the mystical senses. But Moses too received signs from the earth, of which we read in the Psalms: He sent signs and wonders in the midst of you, O Egypt (Ps 134 [135]:9), frogs, locusts, gnats, and the dog-fly; and from heaven hail and fire and darkness of three days. I think that Hezekiah too, when the sun went back ten lines, received a sign from heaven (2 Kgs 20); and Joshua the son of Nun at Gibeon and Aijalon, when the sun and the moon stood still (Josh 10). Most think that Saul received a sign from the earth and from the depth of hell, when he seemed to have raised up Samuel through incantations and magic arts (1 Sam 28). But Jonah the prophet too, freed from the abyss, and from the deep and the jaws of death, gave and received the sign of hell (Jonah 2). I have read in the Commentaries of a certain man that this place was thinned out through allegory, so that he understood the depth and the height as αἰσθητὰ and νοητὰ, which we can call sensible things and intelligible things, of which the one is referred to the senses, the other to the mind and reason. The Virgin too he interprets as the soul which is corrupted by no consciousness of sin, and can bring forth from itself Emmanuel, God with us, that is, the present word of God. But we do not eat the flesh of the lamb boiled (Exod 12), but roasted, and such as can dry up in us all the phlegm of pleasures, lest, while we are wise beyond what we ought to be wise, we neglect the mystery of our faith.

And the Lord spoke again to Achaz. Here the sign of liberation is set out. And first, the liberty to choose a sign is given; second, the sign for believing is conferred: therefore the Lord himself shall give (Isa 7:14). Concerning the first, three things are set out.

But what Isaiah said, "From the height above, or from the depth beneath," was meant to indicate, that "He who descended was the same also who ascended." But in this that he said, "The Lord Himself shall give you a sign," he declared an unlooked-for thing with regard to His generation, which could have been accomplished in no other way than by God the Lord of all, God Himself giving a sign in the house of David. For what great thing or what sign should have been in this, that a young woman conceiving by a man should bring forth,-a thing which happens to all women that produce offspring? But since an unlooked-for salvation was to be provided for men through the help of God, so also was the unlooked-for birth from a virgin accomplished; God giving this sign, but man not working it out.

As far as the wording goes, Ahaz acted modestly when he had been commanded to "ask a sign in the depth or in the height"; and he gave a reason why he was unwilling to "ask," for he said: "I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord." And yet for this modesty he is blamed, and it is said to him: "Hear now, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to offer a contest to men, and how do you offer a contest to the Lord?" Then this promise is spoken: "Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel." Let these things be expounded, and as for the rest we shall look at them as we have need, and in those matters too the grace of God, that they may be made manifest. He is bidden to "ask a sign," not simply, but "for himself"; for the word says: "ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God in the depth or in the height." The "sign" set before him is "the Lord," my Jesus Christ. For this is the "sign" which he is bidden to "ask for himself in the depth or in the height." "In the depth" indeed, because "he who descended is the very same"; but "in the height," because "he who ascended above all the heavens is the very same." Yet to me this "sign" that is set before me, my "Lord" Jesus Christ, "in the depth and in the height," is of no profit, unless the mystery concerning his "depth" and "height" comes to be for me. For when I have received the mystery concerning Christ Jesus, concerning his "depth" and "height," then I shall receive the "sign" according to the commandment of the Lord, and it will be said to me, as to one having in himself "the depth and the height": "Say not in your heart: who shall ascend into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down. Or who shall descend into the abyss? — that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. The word is near you, mighty in your mouth and in your heart." Therefore it is enjoined upon us all that we "ask" this "sign" for ourselves, that the "sign" which "the Lord God gives in the depth and in the height" may become useful to us. But if there is anyone who knows how to use reasonable contemplation, let him recognize this, that what is said, "in the depth and in the height," is not said disjunctively; for it signifies this, that he is able to be both. "Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord in the depth and in the height." And in the promise too the Apostle said: "that we may know what is the depth and the height and the breadth and the length." "And Ahaz says: I will not ask." He was unbelieving; for it was said: "ask for yourself." But the people even to this day does not "ask a sign," and therefore does not have him, and the people "offers a contest to the Lord" — the people that does not receive my Lord Jesus Christ. Then another question follows. For when this man says: "I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord," and reckons it to be a temptation if he "should ask a sign," it is said: "Hear now, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to offer a contest to men, and how do you offer a contest to the Lord?" But he does not "offer a contest to the Lord," nor do I think that he "offers a contest" even "to men," the one who "asks a sign in the depth or in the height." For the "contest" is God's, namely how he may save man. Therefore he does not "offer a contest to the Lord" who "takes refuge in salvation"; but he who, while the Lord contends to save man, flees from salvation and withdraws far from the Lord, "offers a contest to the Lord." "Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel." The true text of the copies of this prophet says: "you shall call." Moreover in Matthew we know it is read: "and they shall call his name Emmanuel." We cannot say that we ought to make anything less of the prophet. But how does the Gospel have this reading? Whether it was by someone who did not understand and ran to the easier course, as has happened also in many other places, or whether perhaps someone might say that the Gospel was published so from the beginning? Let him who wishes deliberate. The prophet indeed manifestly has: "and you shall call his name Emmanuel." I have known a certain man who, reading at the opening of the scriptures of the Gospel, "and you shall call his name Emmanuel," said within himself: 'What is "you shall call"? Who "shall call"? "Ahaz"; and how can "Ahaz" hear concerning the Savior, who came after many generations: "you shall call his name Emmanuel"?' and so, in place of what is, "you shall call," he wrote: "they shall call." But see that it is not to "Ahaz" that it is said: "and you shall call his name Emmanuel," but to the "house of David"; see that it is manifestly said: "Hear now, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to offer a contest to men, and how do you offer a contest to the Lord? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel." If, therefore, at any time we do not understand what has been said, let us make nothing less of it nor run to the easier course, but let us wait for the grace of God to supply to us, through the illumination of knowledge, the explanation of the question — or else, again, let the grace of God, through whom it wills, illumine us, so that we may seek no further, but our question may be resolved; and if we are counted worthy of understanding from the Lord, he will the more readily plead our very cause. What, then, is the "house of David"? If "David" is Christ, as I have often proved, the "house of David" is we, the Church of God; and it is said to us who are the Church, that we should not "offer a contest to the Lord" as said above, but that, when the Lord gives a "sign," we should receive it. To us, not to the "house of David," are these things said. And it is prophesied that, if anyone is of the "house of David," he "shall call his name Emmanuel"; for at the coming of Christ our Church alone says of Christ: "God with us." These things having been explained, as the grace of the Lord has granted, let us now inquire into other riddles.

And He bears a greater than any human name, God with us. And this is why the sign connected with Him is said to have depth, and also height: depth, by reason of His descent to humanity, and His presence here even unto death: height, by reason of the restitution of His divine glory from the depth, or because of the divine nature of His pre-existence.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 1

First, the liberty of choosing a sign is conceded: and the Lord said to Achaz—because he disdained the prophets, the Lord himself spoke: because it seems hard that such powerful kings would be destroyed so quickly—ask you a sign, that you might believe, of the Lord your God. From this it seems that these may be the words of the prophet; and to this is to be said that it is a custom of Hebrew speech to use a noun for a pronoun: hence, of the Lord your God, that is, "of me." Or they are the words of the Lord through inspiration, and of the prophet through declaration, below: should not the prophet seek of his God? (Isa 8:19). Unto the depth of hell, that the earth be opened and hell be exposed, as in the destruction of Dathan and Abiron (Num 16:31–33); or by hell is meant the lower elements, as Moses brought forth locusts and gnats from the earth (Exod 8:16–19, 10:1–20); or unto the height above, as Joshua, when the sun stood still (Josh 10:1–15): for the Jews seek signs (1 Cor 1:22).

And Ahaz said: I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord. It is not of humility but of pride that he will not ask a sign from the Lord. For although it is written in Deuteronomy: You shall not tempt the Lord your God (Deut 6:16), and the Savior used this testimony against the devil (Matt 4), yet, having been ordered to ask, he ought to have fulfilled the command by obedience, especially since both Gideon and Manoah asked for a sign and received it (Judg 6 and 13). And yet, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew speech, in which is written ULO ENASSE ADONAI (ולא אנסה את יהוה), and all have likewise translated I will not tempt the Lord, it can be read I will not exalt the Lord. For the impious king knew that if he asked for a sign he would receive it, and the Lord would be glorified. So, as a worshipper of idols, who had set up altars at every corner of the streets and on the mountains and in the leafy groves, and had fanatics in place of Levites, he will not ask the sign that was commanded.
